a: Greetings, sons and daughters
p: The greeting names no writer, no place and no church. Only a later title calls it "of Barnabas."
b: Most letters of the time open "X to Y, greetings." This one says only "Greetings, sons and daughters." No writer, no city and no church are named anywhere in the twenty-one chapters. The name Barnabas comes from tradition: Lake's Greek text ends with the words "Letter of Barnabas" (21:9), and Lake says Clement of Alexandria quoted the letter as Scripture. Kirsopp Lake, whose Greek the site follows, calls the work "really anonymous" and says the tradition that Paul's companion Barnabas wrote it is "generally regarded as impossible to accept," though "it is convenient to continue to use the title." Lake also says it is either a general treatise or meant for "some community in which Alexandrian ideas prevailed." Address to "sons and daughters" shows the writer wrote for women as well as men.

a: God's decrees
t: "Decrees": the word that runs through the letter
p: Greek dikaiōmata, the righteous requirements God has set. The letter keeps coming back to them.
b: The Greek dikaiōmata are things God has declared right: his requirements, rulings or decrees. Older English says "ordinances." The word frames the whole letter: the readers must "search out the Lord's decrees" (2:1), rejoice in them (4:11), know their wisdom (16:9), and at the end "learn the Lord's decrees, all that are written, and walk in them" (21:1, 21:5). For Barnabas the decrees are not the food laws or the Sabbath read literally, but what God really meant by them. The site keeps one English word, "decrees," every time, so the reader can follow the thread.

a: perfect knowledge
p: Greek gnōsis. The writer wants to add "perfect knowledge" to faith. It is not the "knowledge" of later Gnostic groups.
b: The writer's stated purpose is that "along with your faith you may have perfect knowledge." The Greek is gnōsis, the word later used by the second-century groups called Gnostics, who taught a secret knowledge that saves the soul from the material world. Barnabas is not one of them. His "knowledge" is the hidden meaning of the Scriptures: how the sacrifices, the fasts, the food laws and the Sabbath point to Christ and the church (6:9; 9:8; 10:10; 13:7). He also uses the word for plain moral teaching (18:1; 19:1). He still holds that God made the world (5:5; 6:12) and that the Lord came "in the flesh" (5:6, 5:10-11), the very things later Gnostic teachers denied.

a: There are three teachings of the Lord
t: Three teachings: a passage the copies tangle
p: Lake calls the text here "confused." The Latin has a shorter list. The site follows Lake's text, from C.
b: The word for "teachings" is dogmata, the word behind "dogma," here simply the Lord's basic truths. Lake's footnote says "the text of this whole passage is confused." He prints the form found in the Codex Constantinopolitanus (C), which "gives the best sense, though it is doubtful if it is more than the correction of an early corruption." Codex Sinaiticus has a longer, jumbled list (life, faith, hope, beginning and end), and the Latin has only "the three teachings of the Lord: the hope of life, the beginning and the end." The three as Lake prints them are hope, righteousness and love, each tied to a pair: beginning and end, judgment, gladness. The list recalls the faith, hope and love of 1 Corinthians 13:13. See the variant.

a: the Master
p: Greek despotēs. The site says "Master" for God, as in Luke 2:29 and Acts 4:24.
b: Barnabas calls God ho despotēs, "the Master," here and at 4:3. It is the word for the owner of a household, used for God in Simeon's prayer (Luke 2:29), the church's prayer in Acts 4:24 and the martyrs' cry in Revelation 6:10. The site says "Master" there too. The point is God's full right over his world and its times: in 4:3 the Master is the one who "cut short the times and the days."

a: not as a teacher, but as one of you
p: The writer says three times that he does not write as a teacher. It may be modesty, or a real rule about who could teach.
b: He says it here, again at 4:9 ("not as a teacher") and in effect at 6:5 and 9:9. James warns that not many should become teachers (James 3:1), and in the Didache the "teacher" is a recognized ministry (Didache 13:2; 15:1). The words may be simple modesty, or they may cover a real teaching role, since he claims a gift of knowledge (9:9) and speaks with full authority. Ladeuze (Catholic Encyclopedia) takes the second view: the writer had "exercised the office of a didaskalos," a teacher, in the church he writes to, and was now away from it. Either way, he puts himself beside his readers, "one of you," and that is the tone of the whole letter.

a: the one who is at work has the power himself
p: The writer means the devil, the "evil one" of 2:10, who has power now, in the "lawless time."
b: The Greek is literally "the one who works," with no noun. The next verses make clear it is the devil: "the evil one" (2:10), "the evil ruler" (4:13), "the Black One" (4:9; 20:1), "the ruler of the present time of lawlessness" (18:2). Paul speaks the same way of "the spirit who is now active among those who refuse to obey" (Ephesians 2:2) and of the "power" of the lawless one at work (2 Thessalonians 2:7-9). Barnabas sees his own days as "evil days" under that power, the last days before the end (4:9).

a: he needs no sacrifices
t: Compared with the Bible: did God ever want sacrifices?
p: The prophets said God rejects sacrifice without justice. Barnabas goes further: God never wanted it at all.
b: The prophets whom Barnabas quotes do attack sacrifice (Isaiah 1:11-14; Jeremiah 7:22-23; Psalm 51:16-17; Hosea 6:6; Amos 5:21-24). Read in their setting, they seem to mean that God rejects offerings from people who do wrong and ignore justice, not that the offerings themselves were never his will, since the same Bible commands them (Leviticus 1-7) and the same prophets look forward to right offerings (Isaiah 56:7; Malachi 3:3-4; Psalm 51:19). Barnabas reads them as saying that God "needs" none of it and "did away with" it (2:6). On the first point he agrees with the Bible (Psalm 50:8-13; Acts 17:25). On the second he goes beyond it: the New Testament says the sacrifices were a shadow fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 10:1-10), not a mistake.
r: Isaiah 1:11-14; Jeremiah 7:22-23; Psalm 50:8-13; Psalm 51:16-19; Hosea 6:6; Amos 5:21-24; Hebrews 10:1-10; Acts 17:25

a: What do I want with all your sacrifices?
p: Barnabas quotes the Greek of Isaiah 1:11-13 almost word for word, but leaves out a few words.
b: The quotation follows the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament made before Jesus, of Isaiah 1:11-13. It leaves out "of rams" after "burnt offerings," and stops after "I cannot stand" without the Greek's next words about the fast and the day of rest. The site's Isaiah, made from the Hebrew, reads "What use to me are all your many sacrifices?" and "I am stuffed with rams for burnt offerings" (Isaiah 1:11). Barnabas uses the same verse again at 15:8 to argue that God rejects "the Sabbaths of the present time."

a: the new law of our Lord Jesus Christ
p: Barnabas calls the gospel a "new law." The phrase can be read both as freedom and as a new rulebook.
b: Barnabas calls the faith a "new law." It "has no yoke of force," an echo of Jesus' easy yoke (Matthew 11:29-30) and of Peter's "yoke" that neither the fathers nor we could bear (Acts 15:10). Paul speaks of "the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2) and James of "the complete law, the law of freedom" (James 1:25). Its offering is "not made by human hands": for Barnabas, the true offering is the crushed heart (2:10). The phrase can be heard as freedom from the old yoke, or as a new set of rules, since Barnabas ends with commands to keep (19-21).

a: Did I command your fathers
p: Barnabas joins Jeremiah 7:22-23 to Zechariah 8:17 as if they were one saying.
b: The question form comes from the Greek of Jeremiah 7:22, which says, "I did not speak to your fathers ... about burnt offerings and sacrifice." Barnabas turns it into a question that expects the answer no. Then, where Jeremiah goes on, "Listen to my voice" (Jeremiah 7:23), Barnabas puts in words from Zechariah 8:17: no grudges against a neighbor, and "do not love a false oath." Joining verses this way is common in early Christian writing (compare Romans 3:10-18). The site's Jeremiah 7:22-23 has the Hebrew's sense: God gave "no orders about burnt offering or sacrifice" on the day of the Exodus, but told them to listen to his voice.

a: is a crushed heart
t: A crushed heart, and a saying no Bible has
p: The first half is Psalm 51:17 in Greek. The second half is in no known book.
b: The first line is the Greek of Psalm 51:17 (Psalm 50:19 in the Septuagint), "a sacrifice to God is a crushed spirit," with "heart" for "spirit" and "Lord" where the Greek Psalm has "God." The site's Psalm 51:17, from the Hebrew, says "A broken spirit: that is the sacrifice for God." The second line, "a fragrant smell to the Lord is a heart that gives glory to the one who formed it," is in no book of the Bible. Lake's margin gives no source for it. It may come from a lost collection of sayings, or the writer may have shaped it himself to match the first line.

a: sling us away from our life
p: Greek ekspendonaō, to throw out with a sling.
b: The verb ekspendonaō means to hurl from a sling, the weapon David used against Goliath. The picture is of the evil one slipping in unnoticed and then throwing the believer far out of the life he had. The same "slipping in" (Greek pareisdysis) returns at 4:9: "so that the Black One may not slip in." Jude 4 uses a related verb for false teachers who "slipped in."

a: Why do you fast for me
p: Chapter 3 quotes the Greek of Isaiah 58:4-10 at length, split into what God says "to them" and "to us."
b: The quotation runs from Isaiah 58:4 to 58:10, following the Septuagint closely. Barnabas does something Isaiah does not: he divides it. Verses 4-5, the rejected fast, are said "to them" (3:1); verses 6-10, the fast God chose, are said "to us" (3:3). In Isaiah all of it is said to the same people, Israel, to call them back to justice. The site's Isaiah 58, made from the Hebrew, differs in places ("Is a fast like this the one I would choose" in Isaiah 58:5). Barnabas does not reject fasting itself: the Didache, another early Christian writing, sets fast days (Didache 8:1).

a: the pointing hand
p: Greek cheirotonia, "stretching out the hand," here the finger pointed in scorn or threat.
b: The Greek Isaiah 58:9 has cheirotonia, literally "stretching out of the hand." The site's Isaiah 58:9, from the Hebrew, has "the jabbing finger." In Christian writing the same Greek word later meant the laying on of hands at ordination, but that sense is far from here: Isaiah means the hand raised against a neighbor, in accusation or in force.

a: shipwrecked by joining their law
p: Sinaiticus has "newcomers," C "proselytes." Both probably mean converts to the Jewish law.
b: The writer fears his readers might be "shipwrecked" against "their law" as epēlytoi, "newcomers" (Codex Sinaiticus). C and the Latin have "proselytes," converts to Judaism, and Lake thinks both words mean the same (see the variant). The writer's fear is that Christians might take on the Jewish law as converts do. How real the danger was is argued: Ladeuze (Catholic Encyclopedia) finds that "nothing in the letter excites the suspicion" that the readers "had been exposed to the peril of falling again under the yoke of the Law." This is the first plain hint of the letter's purpose.

a: in his Beloved
p: Barnabas calls Jesus "the Beloved" (3:6; 4:3; 4:8), as Ephesians 1:6 does.
b: The Greek ho ēgapēmenos is used of Christ in Ephesians 1:6, "in the Beloved." The voice at Jesus' baptism calls him "my Son, the beloved" (Matthew 3:17). Barnabas uses the title three times (3:6; 4:3; 4:8). It also appears in the Septuagint as a name for Israel (Deuteronomy 32:15; Isaiah 44:2), so the title the writer gives to Jesus is one the Greek Bible gave to the people.

a: as Enoch says
t: "As Enoch says": a quotation that cannot be found
p: Barnabas names Enoch as Scripture, but no passage of 1 Enoch matches. Lake's margin points to 1 Enoch 89-90.
b: Barnabas writes "it is written, as Enoch says," and then gives no clear quotation. Lake's margin points to 1 Enoch 89:61-64 and 90:17, the seventy shepherds whose deeds are written down, but those verses do not contain these words. The sentence that follows (God has "cut short the times and the days") is close in thought to Mark 13:20, where the Lord shortens the days for the chosen. What matters is the formula: Barnabas cites Enoch with "it is written," the way he cites the Bible. Jude also quotes Enoch (Jude 14-15). 1 Enoch is Scripture today for the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches; at 16:5 Barnabas quotes words much closer to 1 Enoch 89:56 and 89:66.

a: Ten kingdoms will reign on the earth
t: The ten kings and the date of the letter
p: Lake reports attempts to date the letter by counting ten Roman emperors here. He finds neither dating theory "quite satisfactory."
b: Barnabas gives Daniel 7:24 freely ("ten kingdoms" for "ten kings") and then Daniel 7:7-8 in 4:5. He applies it to his own time: the "complete stumbling block" has come near (4:3). Lake writes that the ten kings have been identified with the Roman emperors, giving a date "well within the limits of the first century," "though there is no unanimity as to the exact manner in which the number of the ten Emperors is to be reached." He judges that neither this theory nor the one from 16:3-4 "is quite satisfactory, but neither date is in itself impossible," and puts the letter at "the end of the first or beginning of the second century." Ladeuze (Catholic Encyclopedia) notes that by this count "some critics" put the letter under Vespasian, others under Domitian or Nerva, but answers that "there is nothing to prove that the author considers the prophecy to be already accomplished," and that he "might have taken the words of the prophecy to mean a series of kingdoms instead of a line of kings."

a: fiercer than all
t: Daniel 7 in a form no Bible has
p: Barnabas's Daniel matches neither of the two Greek forms of Daniel exactly.
b: There are two Greek forms of Daniel: the Old Greek and the one named for Theodotion. Barnabas matches neither. His "evil and strong and fiercer than all the beasts" is close to neither Greek of Daniel 7:7, and his "little horn, an offshoot" (Greek paraphyadion, a side-shoot) is his own word. Codex Sinaiticus reads "of the earth" instead of "of the sea" (see the variant). The site's Daniel 7:7-8, from the Aramaic, says the three horns were "pulled out by their roots" before the little one.

a: The covenant is theirs and ours
t: Compared with the Bible: whose is the covenant?
p: Barnabas denies that the covenant belongs to the Jews. Paul says the covenants are theirs (Romans 9:4). This conflicts.
b: Barnabas calls it a sin to say "the covenant is theirs and ours" and claims that Israel lost the covenant at Sinai "once and for all" (4:7-8; 14:1-4). Lake sums up the letter's aim as "to warn Christians against a Judaistic conception of the Old Testament." On this point Barnabas conflicts with the New Testament. Paul says of his fellow Jews, "Theirs is the adoption as children, and the glory, and the covenants" (Romans 9:4), that God has not pushed his people away (Romans 11:1), and that "God does not take back his gifts and his call" (Romans 11:29). Hebrews speaks of a new covenant that makes the first "old" (Hebrews 8:13), but it never says Israel had none. The Catholic Church's Nostra Aetate 4 says that God "holds the Jews most dear for the sake of their Fathers" and that "the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God."

a: when Moses had only just received it
p: Barnabas takes the breaking of the tablets (Exodus 32) as the end of Israel's covenant. Exodus goes on to new tablets.
b: The quotation joins Exodus 34:28 (forty days and nights) and Exodus 31:18 ("stone tablets written by God's own finger"). In 4:8 comes Exodus 32:7 and 32:19, or Deuteronomy 9:12-17: the golden calf and the broken tablets. Barnabas stops there. Exodus does not: Moses prays for the people, God makes new tablets and renews the covenant (Exodus 32:11-14; 34:1-10), and Deuteronomy 10:1-5 tells how the new tablets were kept in the ark. Barnabas tells the story again in 14:2-3 and makes the same point. The Lord's words in 4:8 follow the Greek of Exodus 32:7, where the people "acted lawlessly" (Greek ēnomēsen); the site's Exodus 32:7, from the Hebrew, says they "have ruined themselves." On the reading of the golden calf in Jewish tradition, see the topic.
r: Exodus 31:18; Exodus 32:7-19; Exodus 34:1-10; Exodus 34:28; Deuteronomy 9:9-17; Deuteronomy 10:1-5; 14:2-3

a: sealed into our hearts
t: A covenant written on the heart
p: The broken stone covenant gives way, for Barnabas, to one sealed in the heart, as Jeremiah 31 promised.
b: The image echoes Jeremiah 31:33, "on their hearts I will write it," and Paul's letter "written not in ink but by the Spirit of the living God, not on stone tablets but on tablets that are hearts of flesh" (2 Corinthians 3:3). The difference is that Jeremiah's new covenant is made "with the house of Israel" (Jeremiah 31:31), while Barnabas sets it against Israel.

a: the lowliest of your servants
p: Greek peripsēma, the scrapings rubbed off something. Paul uses the word of himself in 1 Corinthians 4:13.
b: A peripsēma is what is scraped or wiped off, so "scum" or "garbage"; the site's 1 Corinthians 4:13 has "the garbage of everything." Barnabas uses it as a word of humble devotion, "I am your peripsēma," twice (here and 6:5), much as Paul uses it of himself. The Plain English Translation gives the sense, "the lowliest of your servants," rather than the picture.

a: the Black One
t: "The Black One": a name for the devil
p: Greek ho melas. Barnabas names the devil "the Black One" here and at 20:1. The word is about darkness, not skin.
b: Barnabas calls the devil ho melas, "the black one," here and at the start of the way of darkness (20:1). It goes with his light and darkness picture (18:1): the devil is the prince of the dark, as God is light (1 John 1:5). The Latin version leaves out the whole clause here. The name has nothing to do with human skin color; it is about darkness against light. The site renders the Greek as it is and says what it means.

a: as though you were already made right with God
p: Barnabas warns against believers who keep to themselves, as though already safe. Hebrews says the same.
b: The Greek monazete, "live alone," is the root of the later word "monk," but here it means Christians who stay away from the gathering as though they were "already justified" (the verb Paul uses for being declared righteous). Hebrews 10:25 urges believers not to give up meeting together, "as some do." Barnabas's point is that no one is finished yet: the warnings of 4:13-14 follow. The words "as though already justified" can be heard as a warning against a false sense of safety, or as a sign that the writer did not speak of justification the way Paul did.

a: Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes
p: The Greek of Isaiah 5:21, nearly word for word.
b: The site's Isaiah 5:21 reads "Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes / and who seem to themselves to understand!" Barnabas follows the Greek, which says "wise in themselves and clever in their own sight." He turns the woe on any reader who thinks he can do without the community (4:10).

a: Let us become a perfect temple for God
p: The first mention of a theme that fills chapter 16: the believers themselves are God's temple.
b: Paul asks, "Do you not know that you are God's temple, and that the Spirit of God lives in you?" (1 Corinthians 3:16), and Ephesians speaks of the church "growing up as a temple that is holy in the Lord" (Ephesians 2:21). Barnabas returns to the idea at 6:15 and develops it fully in 16:6-10, where the true temple is the believer's heart, not the building in Jerusalem.

a: as people who are already called
p: The "called" may still be lost. That sets up the saying in 4:14.
b: The Greek klētoi, "called," is the word in 4:14's "the called are many." Barnabas warns that being called is not the end of the matter: the evil ruler can still "push us out of the Lord's kingdom." Such warnings are read two ways in the churches' debate on whether the saved can fall away: as meaning that a believer can lose salvation, or as the means God uses to keep his chosen from falling. The letter does not settle that debate; it simply urges watchfulness.

a: as it is written
t: "As it is written": a Gospel saying quoted as Scripture
p: Barnabas introduces the saying found in Matthew 22:14 with "it is written," the formula for Scripture.
b: "Many called, but few chosen" is the closing line of the parable of the wedding feast in Matthew 22:14 (Greek polloi klētoi, oligoi de eklektoi; Barnabas's Greek is the same words without "for" and "are"). Barnabas brings it in with gegraptai, "it is written," the formula he and the New Testament use for the Scriptures of Israel. That may mean he knew Matthew as a written book and counted it as Scripture; Ladeuze (Catholic Encyclopedia) reads it that way: the letter "cites, in fact, the Gospel of St. Matthew as Scripture." It may also mean he took it from a collection of sayings, or thought it came from the Old Testament. The letter does not say which. The site's Matthew 22:14 reads "For the called are many, but the chosen are few."

a: they were still abandoned
p: Barnabas says that after all the signs, Israel was abandoned. Paul says the opposite (Romans 11:1).
b: Barnabas uses Israel as a warning: they saw great signs and were still abandoned, so Christians must not grow careless. Paul uses Israel's story as a warning too (1 Corinthians 10:1-12), but he denies that God has abandoned his people: "did God push his people away? By no means!" (Romans 11:1). The prophets who rebuke Israel also promise that God will not cast it off (Jeremiah 31:35-37). On how churches read Israel's place today, see the topic.

a: sprinkling
p: The phrase looks back to the covenant at Sinai and forward to the red heifer of chapter 8.
b: "The blood of sprinkling" is the phrase of Hebrews 12:24 and 1 Peter 1:2: the blood of Jesus, like the blood Moses sprinkled on the people when the covenant was made (Exodus 24:8; Hebrews 9:19). Barnabas will make sprinkling the center of his reading of the red heifer (8:1-3). The Codex Constantinopolitanus and the Latin smooth the phrase to "his sprinkling of blood"; Lake calls that "a natural correction of the more difficult phrase" (see the variant).

a: and some concern us
p: A key to the letter's method: some words of Scripture are for "them," some for "us."
b: Barnabas reads the prophets as speaking two ways at once: some words "to Israel," usually rebuke, and some "to us," usually promise. He did the same with Isaiah 58 in chapter 3. Paul too says Scripture was written "for our sake" (Romans 4:23-24; 1 Corinthians 10:11), but he never divides it into words for Israel and words for the church. The method lets Barnabas give the blessings to the church and the curses to Israel, though the prophets spoke both the rebuke and the promise to Israel.

a: He was wounded for our lawless deeds
p: Barnabas quotes the Greek of Isaiah 53:5 and 53:7, the Servant who suffers for others.
b: Barnabas swaps the two nouns of the Greek Isaiah 53:5 ("sins" and "lawless deeds") and leaves out a line, then gives Isaiah 53:7 in the same words Acts 8:32 uses. The site's Acts 8:32 is the model for the last sentence, and 1 Peter 2:24 for "by his welts we were healed." The New Testament reads Isaiah 53 of Jesus' death (Acts 8:32-35; 1 Peter 2:22-25). On Jewish and Christian readings of the Servant, see the topic.

a: Not unjustly are nets spread for birds
p: Proverbs 1:17 in the Greek, which says the opposite of the Hebrew.
b: The Greek Proverbs 1:17 reads "not unjustly are nets spread for birds": birds are caught fairly, so a person who knows the right way and still goes wrong deserves his end. The site's Proverbs 1:17, from the Hebrew, says "For nothing the net is spread out / before the eyes of every winged thing": it is useless to set a trap where the bird can see it. Barnabas's argument depends on the Greek.

a: Let us make humankind in our image and likeness
t: "Let us make": God speaking to the Son
p: Barnabas reads the plural "us" of Genesis 1:26 as God speaking to the Son.
b: Barnabas says God said these words to the Lord Jesus "at the founding of the world," and says so again at 6:12: "These words were spoken to the Son." This is an early Christian reading of the plural in Genesis 1:26 as a sign of more than one person in God. Rashi, the medieval Jewish commentator, reads it as God taking counsel with the angels, out of humility, "because the man is in the likeness of the angels and they might envy him" (Rashi on Genesis 1:26, in the Rosenbaum and Silbermann English at Sefaria). See the topic.

a: he had to be revealed in the flesh
p: The letter's key phrase for the Incarnation. It answers people who denied that Christ had a real body.
b: "In the flesh" (Greek en sarki) comes again and again in chapters 5-7 and 12 (5:10, 5:11, 6:7, 6:9, 6:14, 7:5, 12:10). 1 Timothy 3:16 says Christ "was made visible in the flesh," and 1 John 4:2 makes confessing Christ "come in the flesh" the test of true teaching. Barnabas stresses it because his whole argument needs a real suffering body: the scapegoat, the heifer and the bronze snake all point to a death in the flesh. He gives a reason of his own in 5:10: no one could have looked at God unveiled.

a: the new people
p: Barnabas calls the church "the new people." Elsewhere he calls Israel "the first people" (13:1).
b: The phrase ho laos ho kainos is Barnabas's own; the New Testament speaks of "a people for his own possession" (Titus 2:14; 1 Peter 2:9-10) but not of a "new" people. He uses it again at 7:5, and in 13:1 asks "whether this people is the heir, or the first one."
orig: τὸν λαὸν τὸν καινόν (ton laon ton kainon)

a: they were lawless beyond every kind of sin
p: Origen suggests that the pagan critic Celsus may have drawn his charge against the apostles from this line.
b: Barnabas says Jesus chose as apostles men "lawless beyond every kind of sin," to show that he came to call sinners (Matthew 9:13; compare 1 Timothy 1:15). Origen, answering the pagan critic Celsus, writes: "Now in the general Epistle of Barnabas, from which perhaps Celsus took the statement that the apostles were notoriously wicked men, it is recorded that Jesus selected His own apostles, as persons who were more guilty of sin than all other evildoers" (Against Celsus 1.63, in the English of the Ante-Nicene Fathers). So Origen thinks Celsus may have drawn on the letter; he does not say Celsus quoted it. Origen calls the letter "catholic" in the Greek, meaning written for all the churches, as Lake notes. He then points to Paul and Peter, who called themselves sinners (1 Timothy 1:15; Luke 5:8).

a: they cannot look straight into its rays
t: The sun that no one can look at
p: If people cannot look at the sun God made, they could never look at God himself. So he came in the flesh.
b: Barnabas argues from the lesser to the greater: if no one can look straight at the sun, which God made and which "will one day cease to be," no one could look at its maker unveiled. So he came "in the flesh" to be seen. The thought echoes Exodus 33:20 ("no human being can see me and stay alive") and John 1:18 (no one has ever seen God; the Son has made him known). Some copies make it a question; see the variant.

a: to bring to its full total the sins
t: Filling up the total of sins
p: Greek anakephalaioō, "to sum up." Jesus speaks of filling up the measure of the fathers (Matthew 23:32).
b: The verb anakephalaioō means to add up to a final sum; Paul uses it for God summing up all things in Christ (Ephesians 1:10) and the law summed up in love (Romans 13:9). Here the sum is of sins: those who killed the prophets completed their count by killing the Son. The thought is close to Matthew 23:32 ("fill up your fathers' measure!") and 1 Thessalonians 2:15-16. It is one of the passages where the letter's charge against "them" is harshest.

a: When they strike their own shepherd
p: Barnabas changes Zechariah's command into a statement about "them": they strike their own shepherd.
b: In Zechariah 13:7 God commands a sword to strike the shepherd; Jesus quotes it before his arrest (Matthew 26:31: "I will strike the shepherd, and the flock's sheep will be scattered"). Barnabas has "when they strike their own shepherd, then the sheep of the flock will be lost." The change puts the blame on the shepherd's own people. The Greek of Zechariah 13:7 has "strike the shepherds" in the plural.

a: he had to suffer on a tree
p: Greek xylon, wood or tree, the word Deuteronomy 21:23 and the apostles use for the cross.
b: "Tree" (xylon) is the word of Deuteronomy 21:22-23 ("a man who is hanged is cursed by God"), which Paul quotes in Galatians 3:13, and of the apostles' preaching in Acts 5:30 and 10:39 and 1 Peter 2:24. Barnabas keeps the word on purpose. He finds the cross wherever Scripture has wood or a tree (8:5; 11:6-8; 12:1, 12:7).

a: Nail my flesh
p: Two psalms are joined: Psalm 22:20, Psalm 119:120 and Psalm 22:16, all in the Greek.
b: "Spare my life from the sword" is close to the Greek of Psalm 22:20 (Psalm 21:21 in the Septuagint; the site's Psalm 22:20 has "Snatch my life away from the sword"). "Nail my flesh" comes from the Greek of Psalm 119:120, where the psalmist asks God to "nail my flesh with the fear of you"; Barnabas drops "with fear" and so turns a prayer of awe into a picture of the cross. "Gangs of evildoers" is from Psalm 22:16 (Greek "a gathering of evildoers surrounded me"). The last words differ from every Greek Psalm known.

a: I have given my back to the whips
p: The third Servant Song, which the Gospels echo in Jesus' beating and spitting.
b: Barnabas gives the Greek of Isaiah 50:6-7 with small changes, adding "Look" and "I have set," and leaving out "I did not turn my face from shame and spitting." The site's Isaiah 50:6-7 reads "My back I gave to the floggers" and "I have made my face hard as flint." The Gospels tell of Jesus' being struck and spat on in words that recall this song (Matthew 26:67; Mark 14:65; Luke 22:63-64). Barnabas uses "solid rock" again in 6:3 as a sign of Christ's flesh set firm.

a: the Lord's servant
p: Greek pais, "servant" or "child." The site says "servant" for Jesus, as in Acts 3:13.
b: Barnabas changes the Greek of Isaiah 50:8, "let him come near me," into "let him come near the Lord's servant" (tō paidi kyriou). Pais can mean "child" or "servant"; in Isaiah's Greek, "my servant" (ho pais mou, Isaiah 42:1; 52:13) is the Servant of the Lord, and Acts uses the same word for "his servant Jesus" (Acts 3:13; 4:27). The site says "servant" wherever these writers use it of Jesus, following Acts. Barnabas uses the word again at 9:2.

a: a stone of great price, chosen, a cornerstone, held in honor
p: The cornerstone of Isaiah 28:16 and Psalm 118:22, the same pair 1 Peter 2:6-7 uses.
b: Barnabas follows the Greek of Isaiah 28:16 closely and, like 1 Peter 2:6-7, puts it beside Psalm 118:22 (6:4). The early church used these "stone" passages together of Christ (Matthew 21:42; Acts 4:11; Romans 9:33; Ephesians 2:20). The pairing may come from an early collection of proof texts, since 1 Peter has it too. Barnabas adds a twist: the stone was set "for crushing," and he asks whether our hope is in a stone. His answer (6:3) is that the "stone" means Christ's flesh, set in strength.
r: Isaiah 28:16; Psalm 118:22; 1 Peter 2:6-8; Romans 9:33; Ephesians 2:20; Matthew 21:42

a: like bees around a honeycomb
p: Barnabas joins Psalm 22:16, Psalm 118:12 and Psalm 22:18, all read of the cross.
b: "A gang of evildoers surrounded me" is Psalm 22:16 in the Greek; "they circled around me like bees around a honeycomb" is Psalm 118:12 (the site's "They swarmed around me like bees"); "for my clothing they cast lots" is Psalm 22:18, which John ties to the soldiers at the cross (John 19:24; compare Matthew 27:35).

a: Let us tie up the righteous man, because he is a nuisance to us
t: Isaiah 3:10 in the Greek, and Wisdom 2:12
p: The Greek Isaiah 3:10 has "Let us bind the righteous one." The Hebrew says something else.
b: The Greek of Isaiah 3:9-10 reads "Woe to their soul, for they have plotted an evil plan against themselves, saying, 'Let us bind the righteous one, because he is a nuisance to us.'" The site's Isaiah 3:10, from the Hebrew, reads "Say of the righteous: 'Good!'" The Greek translator read the Hebrew letters differently. The same words "because he is a nuisance to us" stand in the Wisdom of Solomon 2:12 ("Let's set a trap for the righteous man, because he is a nuisance to us"), a book in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles; Lake's margin compares it.
r: Isaiah 3:9-10; Wisdom of Solomon 2:12; John 18:12; Acts 3:14

a: the other prophet, Moses
p: Barnabas counts Moses among the prophets and quotes a blend of Exodus 33:1-3 and Leviticus 20:24.
b: Deuteronomy 18:15 and 34:10 call Moses a prophet, and Barnabas calls him "the other prophet." The quotation joins Exodus 33:1, 3 (the land God promised "with an oath to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob," a land "flowing with milk and honey") with words like Leviticus 20:24 ("You will take their soil as your own"). The site's Exodus 33:1 gives the model for "promised with an oath to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob."

a: a human being is earth that suffers
p: The "good land" means Jesus in the flesh, since Adam was made from earth. A pun on Adam and the ground.
b: This is Barnabas's "knowledge" at work. Since Adam was formed from the earth (Genesis 2:7, "from dust of the ground") and a human being is "earth that suffers," the "good land" of the promise points to Jesus revealed "in the flesh." Behind it stands the Hebrew pun of Genesis 2:7, adam made from the adamah, "ground," though Barnabas writes in Greek. The "land flowing with milk and honey" then becomes the believers, new-made (6:11-19). Some copies lack "it says"; see the variant.

a: another type of person
p: Greek typos, the word Barnabas uses for every "figure." Here God makes believers a new kind, a new stamp.
b: Typos is the letter's key word: the scapegoat, the heifer and Moses' arms are each a typos, a "figure" of Jesus (7:7, 7:10-11; 8:1; 12:2, 12:5-6). Here it means the mark left by a stamp: God has stamped the believers anew, "another type," with the souls of children (compare Matthew 18:3). The site renders typos "figure" everywhere except here, where Barnabas plays on the word.

a: when it says to the Son
t: Compared with the Bible: Genesis 1 read as a word to the Son
p: Barnabas reads Genesis 1:26-28 as God speaking to the Son about the new creation, the church.
b: Barnabas joins Genesis 1:26 (with the animals in a different order) to Genesis 1:28 and says both were spoken "to the Son," and that "the Scripture is speaking about us." Genesis itself speaks of the first creation of humankind. The New Testament does say that all things were made through the Son (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16) and that whoever is in Christ is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17), so Barnabas's reading goes beyond Genesis but stays close to the New Testament's use of it. His claim that the command to rule the animals is not yet fulfilled (6:18-19) is close to Hebrews 2:8: "we see that not everything has been put under him yet."

a: Look, I make the last things like the first
t: A saying found in no book
p: No book of the Bible has these words. Revelation 21:5 and 1 Enoch 90:38 are close in thought.
b: Barnabas brings these words in as the Lord's, but no known book contains them. The nearest are Revelation 21:5 ("Look, I am making all things new"), Isaiah 43:18-19 and 65:17, and the sayings of Jesus about the first and the last (Matthew 19:30; Matthew 20:16); Lake's margin gives only the two verses of Matthew. The site's 1 Enoch notes set it beside 1 Enoch 90:38, where at the end humanity becomes again as it was at the beginning. On "the Lord says" or "he says," see the variant.

a: their hearts of stone
p: Ezekiel 11:19 and 36:26 promise to take away the heart of stone. Barnabas applies it to the church.
b: Ezekiel promises Israel's exiles: "I will take the heart of stone out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh" (Ezekiel 36:26; compare Ezekiel 11:19). Barnabas quotes it loosely, in the plural, and explains "them" as "those whom the Spirit of the Lord foresaw," the believers. He adds his own reason: Christ was to be revealed in the flesh and "live in us." Ezekiel spoke to Israel; Barnabas gives the promise to the church.

a: how shall I appear before the Lord my God
p: Barnabas joins a free form of Psalm 42:2 to the Greek of Psalm 22:22, the verse Hebrews 2:12 gives to Christ.
b: The first question is close to Psalm 42:2 ("When will I come and appear before the face of God?"), though no Greek Psalm has these exact words. The answer, "I will praise you in the assembly of my brothers," is the Greek of Psalm 22:22, which Hebrews 2:12 puts in Jesus' mouth: he is not ashamed to call believers brothers. Barnabas adds "and I will sing to you in the middle of the assembly of the saints." The word for assembly, ekklēsia, is the word for "church," so the verse shows the church as the people brought into the good land.

a: A baby is first given life by honey, and then by milk
p: Barnabas says a baby gets honey first, then milk. Tertullian tells of milk and honey given to the newly baptized.
b: Barnabas states the custom himself: a baby "is first given life by honey, and then by milk." He turns it into a picture of new believers, who are "given life" by faith and by the word (compare 1 Peter 2:2, "be hungry for the milk of the word"). The same picture was used at baptism: Tertullian writes that the newly baptized, "taken up (as new-born children)," "taste first of all a mixture of milk and honey" (The Crown 3, in S. Thelwall's English).

a: ruling takes authority
p: Barnabas argues that Genesis 1:28 is not yet fulfilled. It waits for the age to come.
b: Barnabas looks around and sees that humans do not now rule the beasts, the fish and the birds. So, he argues, the promise must be for later, "when we ourselves are made perfect" (6:19). Hebrews 2:8 makes the same observation about Psalm 8, "we see that not everything has been put under him yet," and points to Jesus as the one in whom it begins. 6:17-19 fits the hope of a future reign of the saints on earth (Revelation 5:10; Revelation 20:4-6), which Barnabas develops in 15:4-8; Ladeuze (Catholic Encyclopedia) calls him "a millenarian."

a: who is Lord and is going to judge the living and the dead
t: Judge of the living and the dead
p: An early confession of faith, found in Acts 10:42, 2 Timothy 4:1 and 1 Peter 4:5.
b: The phrase is an early summary of belief about Christ: Peter preaches that God "has marked him out to judge the living and the dead" (Acts 10:42), and 2 Timothy 4:1 and 1 Peter 4:5 say the same. It later became a line of the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds. Barnabas sets it against the suffering: the one who will judge all is the one who was wounded for us.

a: he was given vinegar and gall to drink
p: Barnabas joins the gall of Matthew 27:34 and the sour wine of 27:48, as Psalm 69:21 does.
b: Matthew tells of wine "mixed with gall" offered before the crucifixion (Matthew 27:34) and sour wine on a sponge at the end (Matthew 27:48; John 19:29). Psalm 69:21 has both; its Greek reads "they gave me gall for my food, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink," where the site's Psalm 69:21, from the Hebrew, has "They put poison in my food, / and when I was thirsty they made me drink vinegar." Barnabas puts the two together and then finds them foretold in the priests' practice on the Day of Atonement (7:4-5). "Vinegar" is the cheap sour wine soldiers drank.

a: Whoever does not fast the fast will be cut off by death
p: Leviticus says whoever does not humble himself on the Day of Atonement will be cut off from his people.
b: Leviticus 23:29 reads, in the site's translation, "Any person who does not humble himself on that very day will be cut off from his kin." "Humble himself" was understood as fasting, which is why the Day of Atonement is called "the Fast" (Acts 27:9). Barnabas gives the command in his own words, "will be cut off by death." The Greek Leviticus has "will be destroyed from his people."

a: the figure set up in Isaac, who was offered on the altar
p: Barnabas sees the binding of Isaac as a figure of Christ's sacrifice, as Hebrews 11:17-19 does.
b: In Genesis 22 Abraham lays Isaac on the altar and is stopped; a ram dies in his place. Hebrews 11:17-19 says Abraham "offered Isaac" and received him back "as a figure" (a Greek word related to "figure"). Barnabas calls Isaac's offering a typos that Christ fulfilled. On the binding of Isaac (the Akedah) in Jewish and Christian reading, see the topic.

a: eat the gut unwashed, with vinegar
t: A command found in no Bible
p: No book of the Bible has these words. The Mishnah says that in one case "the Babylonians" ate the atonement goat raw.
b: Barnabas says "the prophet" commands the priests alone to eat the goat's entrails unwashed with vinegar. No passage of the Old Testament says this; Leviticus 16:27 has the sin offering's body burned outside the camp. The Mishnah, the collection of Jewish teaching written down about AD 200, has a rule about the same goat, the one offered as a sin offering: when the Day of Atonement fell on a Friday, the goat was eaten that night, and "the Babylonians" ate it raw, since they were not fussy about their food (Mishnah Menachot 11:7; the English edition at Sefaria explains them as priests who had come from Babylonia). The Mishnah says nothing of unwashed entrails or vinegar. Barnabas gives the rule he cites a Christian meaning: the priests alone eat, while the people fast, as Christ's own people gave him vinegar.

a: my new people
p: Barnabas makes Christ himself speak, explaining the rite to the priests.
b: In 7:5 the speaker is Christ: "you are going to give me gall mixed with vinegar to drink." Barnabas sets his words in the mouth of the one the rite points to, and contrasts "my new people" with "the people" who fast in sackcloth. The words are the writer's own reading, given as the meaning of the law. To a Jewish reader the Day of Atonement was and is a day when all Israel fasts and asks God's forgiveness (Leviticus 16:29-30); Barnabas turns it into a prophecy of the cross.

a: Take two goats, fine ones and alike
p: Leviticus 16 has two goats, one for the LORD and one for Azazel. "Alike" is not in Leviticus.
b: On the Day of Atonement Aaron took two goats; one was offered as a sin offering, and the other, "for Azazel," was sent alive into the wilderness carrying the people's sins (Leviticus 16:7-10, 16:20-22). Barnabas adds that they must be "fine ones and alike" and calls the offered goat "a burnt offering"; Leviticus says "sin offering." Barnabas's point rests on the likeness: the two goats are one Christ, suffering and coming again (7:10).

a: is cursed
p: Leviticus does not call the scapegoat cursed. Barnabas may be thinking of Deuteronomy 21:23 and Galatians 3:13.
b: Leviticus 16 never calls the goat for Azazel "cursed." Barnabas's word epikataratos is the one Paul uses when he quotes Deuteronomy 21:23: "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree" (Galatians 3:13). He also says Christ became "a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13). That is likely the link in the writer's mind: the goat that bears the people's sins and is driven out is cursed, as Christ was.

a: spit on it and stab it
p: Leviticus has no spitting, scarlet wool or bush. The Mishnah has a crimson strip and people pulling its hair.
b: Leviticus 16 says only that a man led the goat into the wilderness. Barnabas adds that all spat on it and stabbed it, that scarlet wool was tied to its head, and that the man took the wool off and laid it on a bush. The Mishnah, written down about AD 200, has parallels. It tells of Babylonian Jews who would pluck at the goat's hair and tell it to go out with their sins, so that a ramp had to be built for it (Mishnah Yoma 6:4). It says the man who sent it split a strip of crimson in two, tied half to a rock and half between the goat's horns, and pushed the goat backward off a cliff (Yoma 6:6), and it reports Rabbi Ishmael's saying that a crimson strip at the Sanctuary turned white when the goat reached the wilderness, as in Isaiah 1:18 (Yoma 6:8). So Barnabas seems to know real customs of the rite, though not in the Mishnah's form.

a: a bush called the rachel
p: The plant's name is uncertain. Lake says the form of the word "can scarcely be right."
b: The copies spell the plant rhachēl (Codex Sinaiticus), rhachil (G) or rhachē (C), and the last clause has an odd form, tēs rhachous. Lake's footnote says this "can scarcely be right, but in face of the evidence can hardly be rejected." Barnabas describes a thorny bush whose shoots people ate in the countryside and whose fruit was sweet. A thorny bush with sweet fruit fits the picture of 7:11. "We are used to eating its shoots" is one of the few places the writer tells us about his own surroundings.

a: the long scarlet robe around his flesh
t: The scarlet robe and the one they pierced
p: Barnabas joins the soldiers' scarlet cloak to the robe of the coming Son of Man in Revelation 1.
b: The soldiers "threw a scarlet military cloak around him" and crowned him with thorns (Matthew 27:28-29). The risen Christ in Revelation 1:13 wears a robe down to the feet, the Greek podērēs, the same word Barnabas uses. And "they will see" the one "we once crucified" recalls Revelation 1:7 and Zechariah 12:10, which John quotes: "They will look at the one they pierced" (John 19:37). So the crowned goat is Christ at his second coming, recognized by those who mocked him. Justin Martyr also reads the two goats as "the two appearances of Christ" (Dialogue with Trypho 40).

a: they will be astonished at how much he is like the goat
p: Barnabas reads both goats as Christ: the one offered is his death, the crowned one his return.
b: The two goats are "alike" so that those who see Christ coming in glory will recognize the one who suffered. Justin Martyr makes the same reading in Dialogue with Trypho 40: one goat sent away and one offered declare "the two appearances of Christ." Hebrews reads the Day of Atonement differently, as a picture of Christ the high priest entering the sanctuary with his own blood once for all (Hebrews 9:11-14, 9:24-28). In Leviticus the goat for Azazel carries Israel's sins away into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:21-22), and the Mishnah tells how it was sent off (Mishnah Yoma 6:4-6); neither makes the goat a figure of a person. See the topic.

a: those who want to see me and lay hold of my kingdom must receive me through hardship and suffering
t: A saying of Jesus found in no Gospel
p: Barnabas gives words of Jesus that no Gospel has. Acts 14:22 is close in thought.
b: "So," he says, introduces words in Jesus' voice: whoever wants to see him and lay hold of his kingdom must receive him through pressure and suffering. No Gospel has them; they are counted among the agrapha, sayings of Jesus outside the Gospels. The closest Bible verse is Acts 14:22: "we must go through many troubles to enter the kingdom of God." The words may be the writer's own summing up of the picture (the wool among the thorns) rather than a saying handed down.

a: men whose sins are complete should offer a heifer
t: The red heifer: what Numbers says, and what Barnabas adds
p: Numbers 19 has a priest, a heifer and a clean man. Barnabas has sinful men, children and wool on wood.
b: In Numbers 19 the heifer is given to Eleazar the priest, slaughtered outside the camp and burned with cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet yarn; a man who is clean gathers the ashes, and a clean person sprinkles the water on the unclean with hyssop (Numbers 19:2-9, 19:17-18). Barnabas has "men whose sins are complete" offer it, children gather the ashes and sprinkle, and the scarlet wool and hyssop are tied around wood. The Mishnah tractate Parah has some of this: it tells of children born and raised in purity, who rode oxen to the spring of Siloam to draw the water, and records Rabbi Yose the Galilean's view that the children had to sprinkle one another (Mishnah Parah 3:2-4); the cedar, hyssop and scarlet wool were wrapped together and thrown into the fire (3:10-11). Barnabas's version is close to such customs, not to Numbers alone.

a: The calf is Jesus
p: Barnabas calls the heifer a "calf" (Greek moschos) when he applies it to Jesus.
b: Numbers and 8:1 have damalis, a heifer, a young female. In 8:2 Barnabas switches to moschos, "calf," a word for a young bull used of sacrifices in Hebrews 9:12 and 9:19. The change lets him apply the figure to Jesus. Hebrews also sets the heifer's ashes beside Christ's blood: if the ashes made the flesh clean, "how much more" will Christ's blood cleanse the conscience (Hebrews 9:13-14).

a: After that, there are no more such men
p: A hard line. The Latin leaves it out. It may mean that the sinners who killed Jesus have no glory left.
b: Lake's footnote says the Latin version leaves out "After that ... sinners." The Greek is terse: "then no longer men, no longer the glory of sinners." Lake renders it "then there are no longer men, no longer the glory of sinners." It may mean that after the sacrifice the sinful "men" have no further part in the rite, so their glory is gone, while the children (the apostles) carry it on. See the variant.

a: There are twelve of them as a witness to the tribes
p: Barnabas ties the twelve apostles to the twelve tribes, as Jesus does in Matthew 19:28.
b: Jesus tells the Twelve they will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matthew 19:28; Luke 22:30), and the new Jerusalem has the tribes' names on its gates and the apostles' names on its foundations (Revelation 21:12-14). Barnabas's numbers do not quite fit his rite: he speaks of twelve here and three children in 8:4. He uses both numbers as "witnesses."

a: As a witness to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
p: Numbers says nothing of three children. Barnabas ties the number to the three patriarchs.
b: The "three children" are not in Numbers 19 or in the Mishnah passage on the children (Mishnah Parah 3:2-4). Barnabas reads the number as a witness to the three fathers, "great in God's sight." The patriarchs come again in 6:8 (the land promised them) and in chapter 13, where Isaac, Jacob and Abraham show which people is the heir.

a: the kingdom of Jesus is on the tree
p: The wool on the tree means that Jesus reigns from the cross.
b: The scarlet wool tied to the wood stands for Jesus' kingdom set "on the tree," the cross (see the note at 5:13). The title over the cross named him king (John 19:19-22), and John's Gospel calls the cross his being "lifted up" (John 12:32). Lake's footnote says Codex Sinaiticus has "on the tree" in one case and C another (xylou, xylō); the sense is the same.

a: healed through the grime of the hyssop
p: The writer says hyssop heals the sick, though its juice is dirty.
b: Hyssop was used for sprinkling in the Bible's rites of cleansing (Exodus 12:22; Leviticus 14:4-7; Numbers 19:18; Psalm 51:7, "Take away my sin with hyssop"), and John says a sponge on hyssop was lifted to Jesus (John 19:29). Barnabas adds a claim about medicine: hyssop's "grime" (Greek rhypos, "dirt") heals the one in pain. He takes it as a sign that the believers will be saved in "evil and filthy days."
orig: τοῦ ῥύπου τοῦ ὑσσώπου (tou rhypou tou hyssōpou)
r: Exodus 12:22; Leviticus 14:4-7; Numbers 19:18; Psalm 51:7; John 19:29; Hebrews 9:19

a: clear to us, but dark to them
t: Clear to us, dark to them
p: Barnabas says Israel could not understand its own rites because it did not listen. Paul uses the image of a veil.
b: Paul says a veil lies over the hearts of Israel when Moses is read, removed in Christ (2 Corinthians 3:14-16), and that "a hardening has come upon part of Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles comes in" (Romans 11:25). Barnabas says only that it is "dark to them" because "they did not listen to the Lord's voice," and he never speaks of a future change. The Mishnah, by contrast, sets these rites out as practice, to be done in careful detail (Mishnah Yoma 6; Mishnah Parah 3).

a: how he circumcised our heart
p: The Bible speaks of circumcising the heart (Deuteronomy 10:16; Jeremiah 4:4) and of uncircumcised ears (Jeremiah 6:10).
b: Barnabas begins with the ears because the Bible speaks of ears that are "uncircumcised," unable to hear (Jeremiah 6:10; Acts 7:51). He strings together verses about hearing: Psalm 18:44 ("The moment their ears hear, they do what I say" in the site's wording, close to the Greek), Isaiah 33:13 and Jeremiah 4:4. Circumcision of the heart is a biblical command (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4) and a theme of Paul (Romans 2:28-29). Barnabas uses it to argue that only that circumcision was ever meant.
r: Psalm 18:44; Isaiah 33:13; Jeremiah 4:4; Jeremiah 6:10; Deuteronomy 10:16; Deuteronomy 30:6; Acts 7:51; Romans 2:28-29

a: Let him listen closely to the voice of my servant
t: A saying joined from Psalm 34 and Isaiah 50
p: The question comes from Psalm 34:12, the answer from Isaiah 50:10, both changed.
b: "Who is the one who wants to live forever?" is close to the Greek Psalm 34:12 ("Who is the man who wants life?"; the site's Psalm 34:12 has "Is there anyone who wants life?"). "Let him listen to the voice of my servant" echoes Isaiah 50:10 in the Greek ("let him listen to the voice of his servant"). Some copies lack "And again the Spirit of the Lord prophesies" (see the variant). The "servant" is again pais, as at 6:1.

a: Hear, you heavens! Listen, earth!
p: Barnabas quotes Isaiah 1:2, 1:10 and 40:3, changing "rulers of Sodom" to "rulers of this people."
b: The first line follows Isaiah 1:2 (in the site's words, "Hear, you heavens! Listen, earth! For the LORD has spoken"), with "these things as a witness" added. Isaiah 1:10 calls on "the rulers of Sodom"; Barnabas has "rulers of this people." The last line joins "Hear, children" to the voice in the wilderness of Isaiah 40:3, which the Gospels apply to John the Baptist (Matthew 3:3).

a: an evil angel was tricking them
t: Compared with the Bible: circumcision from an evil angel?
p: Barnabas says God never meant circumcision in the flesh. Genesis 17 says God commanded it. This conflicts.
b: Barnabas claims that God "said that circumcision was not to be done in the flesh," and that Israel did it because "an evil angel" misled them. Lake sums up the letter's view: "The literal exegesis of the ceremonial law is to him a device of an evil angel who deceived the Jews." This conflicts with the Bible. Genesis 17:9-14 says God himself commanded the circumcision of the flesh as the sign of his covenant with Abraham, and Leviticus 12:3 repeats it. Paul, who argued hardest that Gentile believers must not be circumcised, still says circumcision is of "much" value to the Jew (Romans 3:1-2) and that Abraham received it "as a sign, a seal" from God (Romans 4:11). Ladeuze (Catholic Encyclopedia) reads the charge more narrowly: what the writer calls the devil's work is "this purely material observance of the ceremonial ordinances," keeping the rites without their spiritual meaning. See the topic.
r: Genesis 17:9-14; Leviticus 12:3; Romans 3:1-2; Romans 4:11; Galatians 5:2-6; Acts 15:1-29

a: here I find a commandment
p: Barnabas quotes Jeremiah 4:3-4, Deuteronomy 10:16 and Jeremiah 9:26, with his own aside.
b: "Do not sow among thorns. Be circumcised for your Lord" is Jeremiah 4:3-4. "Circumcise your hard hearts, and do not harden your neck" is the Greek of Deuteronomy 10:16, which has "hardness of heart" where the Hebrew (and the site's Deuteronomy 10:16) has "the foreskin of your heart." The last is Jeremiah 9:26: "all the nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart." The aside "here I find a commandment" shows the writer reading for the true command behind the words. In Jeremiah 9:25-26 the point is that circumcised Israel will be punished with the uncircumcised nations, because the heart matters; Barnabas uses it to deny the value of circumcision at all.

a: every Syrian and Arab is circumcised too
p: Barnabas argues that circumcision proves nothing, since Syrians, Arabs, Egyptians and pagan priests do it.
b: Circumcision was not only an Israelite custom. Jeremiah 9:25-26 names Egypt, Edom, Ammon and Moab among the circumcised. Josephus says the Arabs "circumcise after the thirteenth year, because Ismael, the founder of their nation," was circumcised at that age (Jewish Antiquities 1.214; Genesis 17:25). Barnabas uses such facts to deny that circumcision marks God's people. Paul makes a related point from the opposite side: Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised (Romans 4:9-12).

a: eighteen and three hundred men
p: Genesis never says Abraham circumcised 318 men. Barnabas joins Genesis 14:14 to Genesis 17:23-27.
b: The number 318 comes from Genesis 14:14, Abraham's "trained men, born in his household, three hundred and eighteen of them," who rescued Lot. The circumcision of all the males of his household is Genesis 17:23-27, which gives no number. Barnabas joins the two. In Greek, letters stood for numbers: I (iota) was 10, H (eta) 8, and T (tau) 300. The Greek writes the number as "ten and eight and three hundred," so the first letters spell IH, the first two letters of IĒSOUS, Jesus, and T has the shape of the cross. Clement of Alexandria repeats the reading: the letter for 300 is in shape "the type of the Lord's sign," and "the Iota and the Eta indicate the Saviour's name" (Stromata 6.11).

a: He names the eighteen first
p: Counting letters (gematria) was used by Jews and Christians. Barnabas uses it for the name of Jesus.
b: Reading the number value of letters is known from Revelation 13:18 ("the number of the beast ... is 666") and from later Jewish interpretation, where it is called gematria. Barnabas's form only works in Greek, and only with the Greek order "ten and eight and three hundred" (the Hebrew of Genesis 14:14 puts the eighteen first too). Barnabas treats it as a gift of knowledge and says no one has learned a truer lesson from him (9:9). Lake notes that the writer "carries a symbolical exegesis as far as did Philo; indeed he goes farther."

a: he received three teachings in his understanding
t: The food laws as moral lessons
p: Barnabas says Moses forbade pigs, birds of prey and scaleless fish to teach three moral lessons, not a diet.
b: Barnabas lists animals from Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 and says each stands for a kind of person to avoid: the pig for people who remember God only when hungry (10:3), birds of prey for robbers (10:4), and fish of the deep for the hopelessly ungodly (10:5). Jewish writers in Alexandria had already read the food laws this way while still keeping them: Philo calls the clean animals' signs "symbols of instruction" (On the Special Laws 4.106). The difference is that Barnabas says Moses never meant the laws to be kept as food rules at all (10:2, 10:9).

a: And I will set out my decrees before this people as a covenant
t: A Deuteronomy verse no Bible has
p: Barnabas cites Deuteronomy, but no verse there matches. It sounds like Deuteronomy 4:1, 4:5 and 4:13.
b: No verse of Deuteronomy has these words. Lake's margin compares Deuteronomy 4:1 and 4:5, where Moses teaches Israel God's "decrees" (the Greek dikaiōmata). Deuteronomy 4:13 joins covenant and commandments. Barnabas argues from it that God's commandment "is not about not eating": the decrees are the moral meaning.

a: So God's commandment is not about not eating
t: Compared with the Bible: were the food laws meant to be kept?
p: Leviticus 11 plainly commands what to eat. Barnabas says it was never meant as food. This goes beyond and against the Old Testament.
b: Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 are rules about food, and Jews kept them and still keep them; Daniel and the Maccabean martyrs were praised for keeping them (Daniel 1:8; 2 Maccabees 7). Barnabas's claim that they were never about eating conflicts with these books. The New Testament takes a different route to Christian freedom: Jesus "made all foods clean" (Mark 7:19), Peter's vision tells him not to call unclean what God has cleansed (Acts 10:15), and Paul says nothing is unclean in itself (Romans 14:14). These passages say the law was given and is now set aside or fulfilled, not that it was misunderstood from the start. On how churches read the food laws, see the topic and its cards at Leviticus 11 and Romans 14.
r: Leviticus 11:1-47; Deuteronomy 14:3-21; Daniel 1:8; Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15; Romans 14:14; Colossians 2:16-17

a: people who are like pigs
p: The pig stands for people who forget God when they are full and cry out to him when hungry.
b: The picture matches Deuteronomy 8:10-14 and Deuteronomy 32:15 ("Jeshurun grew fat, and he kicked"), and Proverbs 30:8-9, which asks for neither poverty nor riches "or else I may be full and deny you." No book of the Bible has the saying that the pig does not know its master; compare Isaiah 1:3, "An ox knows the one who owns it." Pigs were the plainest mark of the food laws for Jews and Gentiles alike (1 Maccabees 1:47; 2 Maccabees 6:18).

a: the eagle, or the hawk, or the kite, or the crow
p: Birds that live by seizing others' food stand for robbers who will not work.
b: The birds are from Leviticus 11:13-19 and Deuteronomy 14:12-18. Barnabas reads them as people who "do not know how to get their food by work and sweat" but seize what belongs to others. Philo too reads the signs of clean and unclean animals as lessons for the soul (On the Special Laws 4.106-109). The thought of working with one's own hands is Paul's (Ephesians 4:28; 2 Thessalonians 3:10-12).

a: the moray eel, or the octopus, or the cuttlefish
p: The scaleless sea creatures that live on the bottom stand for the ungodly, "already condemned."
b: Leviticus 11:9-12 forbids anything in the water without fins and scales. Barnabas names three such creatures, the moray, the octopus and the cuttlefish, and says they live on the ground at the bottom of the deep instead of swimming freely. They stand for people "ungodly to the end." On "cling to," see the variant.

a: For the hare adds to its rear opening every year
t: The hare, the hyena and the weasel
p: Barnabas uses ancient animal lore. Clement of Alexandria repeats the hare and hyena lore but rejects it.
b: The hare is in Leviticus 11:6 and Deuteronomy 14:7. The hyena (10:7) is not in either list in the site's translation, though Clement of Alexandria quotes Moses as forbidding "the hare and the hyena" (Instructor 2.10, a passage the Ante-Nicene Fathers translation at New Advent leaves in Latin). The weasel is in Leviticus 11:29. Barnabas's facts about them were popular lore: the hare grows a new opening each year, the hyena changes sex, the weasel conceives through its mouth. Clement reports the same about the hare and the hyena as what "they say," accepts that Moses meant these animals as signs of vices, but rejects the explanation, because "nature never can be forced to change" (Instructor 2.10).

a: one who abuses boys
p: Greek paidophthoros, a corrupter of boys. The Two Ways forbids it again at 19:4.
b: The Greek paidophthoros means one who "corrupts" or abuses boys, the common practice of men taking boys as sexual partners in the Greek and Roman world. The Two Ways forbids the act with the verb, "You must not sexually abuse boys" (19:4), the wording of Didache 2:2. In 10:7 the related phthoreus, set beside "adulterer," is "a seducer"; in the Two Ways the same word, with "what God has formed" as its object, is "destroyers" (20:2), as in Didache 5:2.

a: do lawless things with the mouth
p: The writer means a sexual act. He states it briefly and does not dwell on it.
b: The phrase refers to oral sex, which the writer condemns as impure. He says it in a few covering words and moves on. The animal lore behind it is that the weasel conceives through the mouth.

a: as if they were about eating
p: Barnabas says Israel took the food laws literally because of the desire of the flesh.
b: Barnabas blames the literal keeping of the food laws on "the desire of the flesh," as if the Jews kept them out of appetite. It is a harsh charge, and odd, since the laws restrict eating. Jewish teaching saw keeping them as obedience and holiness: "be holy, for I am holy" (Leviticus 11:45). On the site's cards about whether Christians should keep them, see the topic.

a: And David receives knowledge of the same three teachings
t: Psalm 1 as a key to the food laws
p: Barnabas maps the three lines of Psalm 1:1 onto the fish, the pig and the birds.
b: Psalm 1:1 has three negatives: not walking, not standing, not sitting. Barnabas matches each to one of his three animals. The site's Psalm 1:1 supplies the wording for the first two lines. The third line in the Greek Psalm says "the seat of pests" (loimōn), where the Hebrew and the site's Psalm 1:1 have "where mockers sit"; Barnabas needs the Greek word, which he has just used of the birds in 10:4.

a: chew the cud of the Lord's word
t: Chewing the cud and the split hoof
p: Cud-chewing means thinking the word over. The split hoof means living in this world while waiting for the next.
b: Animals that chew the cud and have a split hoof are clean (Leviticus 11:3; Deuteronomy 14:6). Barnabas reads chewing the cud as meditating on the word, and the split hoof as the righteous walking in this world while awaiting "the holy age." Philo had read the same two signs the same way: the cud-chewer stands for the student who goes over what he has heard and fixes it in memory, and the parted hoof for telling apart the two roads of life, "the one road leading to wickedness and the other to virtue" (On the Special Laws 4.107-108). Barnabas may have known this Alexandrian Jewish reading; Lake compares his method to Philo's.

a: he circumcised our hearing and our hearts
p: Barnabas claims only Christians understand the law. Deuteronomy says the law is near, and meant to be done.
b: "How could they understand?" closes the chapter on the food laws. For Barnabas, only those whose ears and hearts God has circumcised (9:1-3) can read the law rightly. Deuteronomy itself says the law is near and meant to be done: "The word is close by you, very close: in your mouth and in your heart, for you to do" (Deuteronomy 30:14). The New Testament itself treats the law as holy and given by God (Romans 7:12) and fulfilled in Christ (Matthew 5:17), not as a riddle Israel misread. See the topic on allegorical reading.

a: they would not accept the baptism that brings forgiveness of sins
p: Barnabas finds baptism in the water of the prophets and says Israel would refuse it.
b: Chapter 11 reads Old Testament water passages as baptism. "Baptism that brings forgiveness of sins" echoes Acts 2:38 and Mark 1:4. That Israel would "build something for themselves" may mean their own washings (Mark 7:3-4; Hebrews 6:2 speaks of "teaching about washings") or the cisterns of Jeremiah 2:13, quoted next. On how churches differ about what baptism does, see the topic and its cards at Acts 2 and Mark 16.

a: the spring of life
p: The Greek Jeremiah has "the spring of the water of life"; Barnabas makes the cisterns "a pit of death."
b: Jeremiah 2:13 in the site's words: "me they have left, the spring of living water, to dig themselves cisterns, cisterns full of cracks." Barnabas shortens it and changes the cisterns to "a pit of death," so that the contrast is life and death, as in his Two Ways (18-20). Jesus speaks of "living water" (John 4:10-14; 7:37-39).

a: Is my holy mountain Sinai a deserted rock?
p: The Greek Isaiah 16:1 asks whether the mountain of daughter Zion is a desert rock. Barnabas puts Sinai.
b: The Greek of Isaiah 16:1-2 reads: "Is the mountain of daughter Zion a desert rock? For you will be like the young of a bird flying up, its nest taken away." Barnabas changes Zion to "my holy mountain Sinai," perhaps because his theme is the law given at Sinai and the rock that gave water in the desert (Exodus 17:6; 1 Corinthians 10:4). The site's Isaiah 16:1, from the Hebrew, is quite different: a call to send a lamb to the hill of Daughter Zion.

a: I will go ahead of you and level the mountains
p: Words to Cyrus (Isaiah 45) and to the righteous (Isaiah 33) read as a promise of baptism.
b: 11:4 is Isaiah 45:2-3, God's words to Cyrus, in the Greek. 11:5 is the Greek of Isaiah 33:16-18: the righteous will live "in a high cave of strong rock," his "water will not fail" (Greek "his water is faithful"), he will see "a king in glory." Barnabas reads the rock as Christ and the water as baptism. The site's Isaiah 33:16 has "his water will hold out."

a: like a tree set out by channels of water
t: Psalm 1:3-6: the tree and the water
p: Psalm 1 in the Greek, with a few changes. Barnabas finds in it both the water and the cross.
b: The site's Psalm 1:3-6 gives the wording where the Greek matches: "a tree set out by channels of water," "all that he does turns out well," "the Lord knows the road of the righteous, but the road of the wicked will be lost." Where the Greek differs Barnabas follows it: "in its season," "its leaf will not fall off," "like the dust" (Hebrew "husks"), "will not rise up in the judgment." In 11:8 he explains: the tree is the cross, the water is baptism.

a: Happy are those who put their hope in the cross and went down into the water
p: Barnabas joins the cross and baptism, as Paul does in Romans 6.
b: For Barnabas, Psalm 1 joins the tree (the cross) and the water (baptism): blessed are those who hope in the cross and went down into the water. Paul too ties baptism to Christ's death: "By baptism into death, then, we were buried with him" (Romans 6:4; compare Colossians 2:12). The leaf that does not fall is every word spoken "in faith and love" that turns others to God. Churches differ on whether baptism itself brings forgiveness, as 11:1 and 11:11 seem to say; see the cards at Acts 2.

a: And the land of Jacob was praised above every land
p: No verse has these words. Lake's margin points to the Wisdom of Solomon.
b: Barnabas says "another prophet" says this, but no book has it in this form. Lake's margin points to the Wisdom of Solomon, a book in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles; there Wisdom 8:20, where a good soul says "I came into a body without stain," fits the "vessel of his Spirit" that follows. The site adds two prophets: Zephaniah 3:19 promises to make the scattered "a praise and a name," and Ezekiel 20:6 calls the land "the Beautiful Land, above all lands." Barnabas reads "the land" as the body, "the vessel of his Spirit," as he read the good land as the flesh in 6:9.

a: And there was a river flowing on the right
p: A loose summary of Ezekiel 47:1-12, the river flowing from the Temple, with trees whose fruit gives life.
b: Ezekiel sees water flowing from the right side of the Temple, becoming a river, with trees on both banks whose fruit is food and whose leaves heal (Ezekiel 47:1-12). Revelation 22:1-2 takes up the same picture. Barnabas's "whoever eats from them will live forever" is not in Ezekiel; it recalls the tree of life (Genesis 3:22; John 6:51). He reads the river as baptism and the fruit as faith (11:11).

a: we go down into the water
p: Barnabas describes baptism as going down into water and coming up again, as Acts 8:38-39 does.
b: "We go down ... and come up" is the language of baptism in water deep enough to go into, as with the Ethiopian official: "The two of them went down into the water" (Acts 8:38), and "they came up from the water" (Acts 8:39) and Jesus (Mark 1:10). Whether this means full immersion or standing in water while it is poured is argued; see the site's card at Acts 8. The Didache allows pouring when there is not enough water (Didache 7:3).

a: When a tree is bent down and stands up again, and when blood drips from a tree
t: A prophecy from outside the Bible
p: No book of the Bible has this. Lake's margin points to 4 Ezra 4:33 and 5:5, where blood drips from wood.
b: Barnabas cites "another prophet" for this, but it is in no book of the Bible. Lake's margin points to 4 Ezra (2 Esdras) 4:33 and 5:5. 4 Ezra is a Jewish apocalypse written after the Temple's fall in AD 70; among its signs of the end, 5:5 says that blood will drip from wood. It is a book outside the 66 that the site lists among those some Orthodox churches hold. Barnabas reads the bent and rising tree and the dripping blood as the cross.

a: stretches out his hands
p: In Exodus 17 Israel wins while Moses' hands are raised. Barnabas reads his outstretched arms as the cross.
b: In Exodus 17:8-13, while Moses held up his hands, Israel defeated Amalek; when he lowered them, Amalek won, so Aaron and Hur held them up. Barnabas adds details Exodus does not have: Moses piled one weapon on another and stood "higher than all," with his arms stretched out. In the stretched-out arms he sees "a figure of the cross and of the one who was going to suffer." The lesson: Israel could not be saved "unless they hope in him" (12:3). On "to Moses" or "in Moses," see the variant.

a: All day long I have spread out my hands
p: Paul quotes the same verse of Israel in Romans 10:21. Barnabas reads the spread hands as the cross.
b: Isaiah 65:2 in the Greek: "I spread out my hands all day long to a disobedient and contrary people." Paul applies it to Israel in Romans 10:21. Barnabas sees in it the outstretched arms of the cross. He has "who speak against my righteous way," where the Greek Isaiah goes on to "those who walk in a way not good." On the form of "disobedient," see the variant.

a: the transgression came about through the snake in Eve
p: Numbers 21 tells of the snakes and the bronze snake. Barnabas links the snakes to Eden.
b: In Numbers 21:6-9 the LORD sent snakes among the complaining people, and Moses made a bronze snake on a pole; anyone bitten who looked at it lived. Barnabas adds that the snakes fit the sin, since "the transgression came about through the snake in Eve" (Genesis 3:1-13; 2 Corinthians 11:3; 1 Timothy 2:14). Jesus uses the bronze snake as a picture of his being lifted up (John 3:14-15).

a: You are not to have any cast or carved image as a god
t: Compared with the Bible: Moses breaks his own rule?
p: Barnabas notes that Moses, who forbade images, made the bronze snake. The Bible does not see a conflict.
b: The quotation is close to Deuteronomy 27:15 and the second commandment (Exodus 20:4). Barnabas points out what looks like a contradiction and resolves it: Moses made the image "to show a figure of Jesus." In Numbers 21:8 God himself commands the snake, so the Bible treats it as God's provision, not Moses' idea. Later, when Israel burned incense to it, Hezekiah broke it to pieces (2 Kings 18:4), which shows how an image given for healing could become an idol. Christians who use images in worship and those who reject them have both appealed to this snake; see the topic on idols and images.

a: Let him believe and hope that, though it is dead, it can give life
t: The snake that is dead gives life
p: Barnabas adds words to Numbers 21:8: the bitten must believe that the dead snake gives life.
b: In Numbers 21:8 the bitten person only has to look. Barnabas has Moses say: come to the snake on the tree, "believe and hope that, though it is dead, it can give life." The bronze snake on the pole becomes a figure of the dead Christ on the tree, who gives life. "All things are in him and for him" echoes Colossians 1:16 and Romans 11:36.

a: Jesus son of Nun
p: In Greek, Joshua and Jesus are the same name, Iēsous. Barnabas makes much of Moses giving it.
b: The Hebrew Yehoshua (Joshua) and Yeshua (Jesus) are forms of one name, "the LORD saves," and the Greek writes both Iēsous. So Greek readers of Exodus and Joshua read "Jesus son of Nun" (Greek Nauē). Moses renamed Hoshea son of Nun "Joshua" when he sent him to spy out the land (Numbers 13:16), which is the moment Barnabas means in 12:9. The Plain English Translation keeps "Jesus son of Nun" here because the writer's point depends on the name; the site's Hebrews 4:8, where the same Greek name means Joshua, says "Joshua."

a: the Son of God will cut off the whole house of Amalek by the roots
p: In Exodus God says he will wipe out the memory of Amalek. Barnabas makes it the Son of God at the end.
b: Exodus 17:14 in the site's words: "Write this down in the scroll as a reminder, and read it aloud to Joshua: I will wipe out, yes, wipe out the memory of Amalek." Barnabas puts it at the sending of the spies (Numbers 13) and changes the speaker's promise into "the Son of God will cut off the whole house of Amalek by the roots in the last days." Deuteronomy 25:17-19 makes blotting out Amalek a lasting charge to Israel; Barnabas makes the Son of God the one who carries it out at the end.

a: not a son of man but the Son of God
t: Compared with the Bible: not David's son?
p: Barnabas says David "does not call him son" (12:11). The New Testament calls Jesus the son of David again and again.
b: Barnabas uses Psalm 110:1 the way Jesus does in Mark 12:35-37 and Matthew 22:41-45: if David calls the Christ "Lord," how is he his son? In the Gospels the question shows that the Christ is more than David's son, not that he is not his son; Matthew opens by calling Jesus "the son of David" (Matthew 1:1), and Paul says that "according to the flesh," he "came from the offspring of David" (Romans 1:3). Barnabas's conclusion, that David "does not call him son" (12:11), goes beyond the Gospels and seems to conflict with Romans 1:3 and 2 Timothy 2:8. He may mean only that "son of David" is too small a title; the text does not say. Ladeuze (Catholic Encyclopedia) thinks that here (he names 12:10) the writer has the Ebionites in mind, Jewish Christians who held Jesus to be only a man. On the word order of "Christ is David's son" in the copies, see the variant.
r: Psalm 110:1; Mark 12:35-37; Matthew 22:41-45; Matthew 1:1; Romans 1:3; 2 Timothy 2:8; Acts 2:34-35

a: The Lord said to my Christ, the Lord
p: The Greek Isaiah 45:1 says "to my anointed, Cyrus" (Kyrō). Barnabas reads Kyriō, "Lord."
b: Isaiah 45:1 in the Greek reads tō christō mou Kyrō, "to my anointed, to Cyrus," the Persian king who let the exiles go home (the site's Isaiah 45:1: "to his anointed, to Cyrus"). Barnabas has kyriō, "Lord": one letter different. So the verse becomes "the Lord said to my Christ, the Lord," a second proof that the Christ is Lord. Whether Barnabas found this reading in his copy or made the change himself, the proof rests on a single letter.
orig: τῷ Χριστῷ μου κυρίῳ (tō Christō mou kyriō)

a: whether this people is the heir, or the first one
p: Barnabas asks whether the church or Israel inherits the covenant, and answers: the church alone.
b: This is the question of the whole second half of the letter's "knowledge." Barnabas answers it from three stories in Genesis, where the younger is chosen over the elder: Jacob over Esau (13:2-3), Ephraim over Manasseh (13:4-6), and Abraham as father of believing nations (13:7).
