Paul uses the first and last of these too (Romans 9:10-13; Romans 4:11-17; Galatians 4:21-31), but to show that God's choice rests on promise, not birth, and he goes on to say that the promise to Israel still stands (Romans 11:28-29). Barnabas uses them to say the covenant is "for us" and not "for them." See the canon note at 4:6.

a: the greater will serve the lesser
p: Greek ho meizōn, "the greater" or "the elder." Romans 9:12 has the same Greek; the site there says "the elder."
b: The Greek of Genesis 25:23, ho meizōn douleusei tō elassoni, can mean "the elder will serve the younger" or "the greater will serve the lesser." The site's Romans 9:12, which quotes the same Greek, says "The elder will serve the younger," and the site's Genesis 25:23, from the Hebrew, says the same. The Plain English Translation keeps "greater" here and in 13:5 because Barnabas uses the same Greek word, meizōn, in 13:3, "this people is greater than that one," in a second sense. In the quotation "the greater" is the elder brother, the people who will serve. In 13:3 "greater" means higher in God's choice, and Barnabas gives that place to the younger people, the church. One Greek word carries both senses, and the argument turns on it.
orig: ὁ μείζων δουλεύσει τῷ ἐλάσσονι (ho meizōn douleusei tō elassoni)

a: Isaac prayed for Rebekah his wife
p: Barnabas follows the Greek of Genesis 25:21-23 closely. Paul quotes the same oracle in Romans 9:12.
b: Genesis 25:21-23 tells how Isaac prayed for his barren wife, Rebekah conceived twins, went to ask the LORD, and heard that two nations were in her womb. Paul quotes the oracle in Romans 9:10-12 to show that God chose Jacob when "the children had not yet been born, and had not done anything good or bad" (Romans 9:11). Genesis itself calls Esau Edom, the people of the elder twin (Genesis 36:1); Barnabas reads the elder as Israel and the younger as the church.

a: Jacob crossed his hands
p: Genesis 48:13-20: Jacob crosses his hands and blesses the younger. Barnabas adds Genesis 25's words.
b: Barnabas retells Genesis 48: Joseph places Manasseh, the firstborn, at Jacob's right hand, but Jacob crosses his hands and puts his right on Ephraim. In Genesis, Jacob answers Joseph's protest, "I know, my son, I know," and says the younger "will be greater than he" (Genesis 48:19). Barnabas gives him the words of Genesis 25:23 instead, "the greater will serve the lesser," tying the two stories together. He calls the scene "a figure ... of the people to come."

a: the father of the nations who believe in God while uncircumcised
p: Barnabas joins Genesis 15:6 and 17:5 and adds "while uncircumcised," as Paul argues in Romans 4.
b: "When he alone believed and was set down as righteous" is Genesis 15:6 ("he reckoned it to him as righteousness"). "I have made you the father of the nations" is Genesis 17:5, which Paul quotes in Romans 4:17. The words "who believe in God while uncircumcised" are not in Genesis; they are Paul's point in Romans 4:10-12: Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised, so he is "the father of every believer who is uncircumcised." Barnabas puts Paul's conclusion into God's mouth. Paul also calls Abraham the father of the circumcised who follow his faith (Romans 4:12); Barnabas leaves that out.

a: He has given it. But they were not worthy to receive it
t: Compared with the Bible: given but never received?
p: Barnabas says God gave the covenant but Israel never received it. The Old Testament says Israel did receive it.
b: Barnabas grants that God gave the covenant he swore to the fathers, but says the people "were not worthy to receive it," so it passed to the church (14:4). The Old Testament tells it differently: after the golden calf, God renewed the covenant with Israel at Moses' prayer (Exodus 34:1-10, 34:27-28), and the prophets promise a new covenant "with the house of Israel" (Jeremiah 31:31-34). Paul counts the covenants among Israel's gifts (Romans 9:4). So this conflicts with the Bible. Ladeuze (Catholic Encyclopedia) sums up the letter's view: "the Jews never received the divine covenant because they never understood its nature." See the note at 4:6 and the topic.

a: written in the Spirit by the finger of the Lord's hand
p: Barnabas retells 4:7-8: the forty days, the tablets and the golden calf, with "in the Spirit" added.
b: The story comes from Exodus 24:18, 31:18 and 32:7-19 and Deuteronomy 9:9-17 (see the note at 4:7). Barnabas adds that the tablets were written "in the Spirit," which makes the point of 2 Corinthians 3:3 and 3:6 ("the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life").

a: Moses received it as an attendant
t: Moses the attendant, the Lord the giver
p: The contrast of Moses the attendant and Christ the Son is the argument of Hebrews 3:5-6.
b: The Greek therapōn, "attendant" or "servant," is the word the Greek Bible uses of Moses in Numbers 12:7, and Hebrews 3:5 quotes it: "Moses was faithful in the whole of God's house as an attendant," while "Christ, though, is faithful as a Son" (Hebrews 3:6). Barnabas makes the same contrast: Moses received the covenant as an attendant; "the Lord himself" gave it to us, "by enduring suffering for our sake."

a: so that they would reach the full measure of their sins
p: Barnabas says Christ came partly so that "they" would complete their sins. Compare 5:11 and 1 Thessalonians 2:16.
b: As at 5:11, Barnabas gives Christ's coming a double purpose: to complete the sins of "those" who rejected him, and to give the covenant to "us." 1 Thessalonians 2:16 speaks of those who "always fill up the measure of their sins." Unlike Paul in Romans 11, Barnabas never adds a hope for Israel. See the topic on anti-Judaism.

a: a covenant for the human race and a light for the nations
p: The Greek of Isaiah 42:6-7, which says "a covenant of the race," where the Hebrew says "a covenant of the people."
b: Barnabas quotes the Greek of Isaiah 42:6-7. Its diathēkē genous, "covenant of a race," stands where the Hebrew and the site's Isaiah 42:6 have "a covenant of the people." In Isaiah the words are said to the Servant of the LORD. Simeon applies "a light for the nations" to the baby Jesus (Luke 2:32). Barnabas reads it as the Father's command to the Son to ransom "us" from darkness.

a: I have set you as a light for the nations
p: The same Greek words Paul and Barnabas quote in Acts 13:47. The site's Acts 13:47 gives the wording.
b: Barnabas's form of Isaiah 49:6 matches Acts 13:47, where Paul and Barnabas, Paul's companion, turn to the Gentiles in Pisidian Antioch: "I have set you as a light for the nations, so that you may be salvation to the farthest end of the earth." The closing words, "This is what the Lord says, the God who ransomed you," come from Isaiah 49:7. Sharing a quotation with a speech of Paul and Barnabas in Acts says nothing certain about who wrote the letter.

a: to tell the good news of grace to the lowly
p: Jesus reads Isaiah 61 in Nazareth (Luke 4:18-19). Barnabas's copies differ on "the poor" and "the lowly."
b: Isaiah 61:1-2 is the passage Jesus reads in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:18-19). The Greek Isaiah says "to tell the good news to the poor" (ptōchois), and so does Luke. Barnabas's copies differ between "the poor" and "the lowly" (see the variant). Barnabas keeps "the day of repayment," which Jesus stops short of in Luke 4:19.

a: with clean hands and a clean heart
t: A Sabbath command with Psalm 24 added
p: The Ten Words say "remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy." Barnabas adds "with clean hands and a clean heart."
b: Exodus 20:8 and Deuteronomy 5:12 command Israel to keep the Sabbath holy. Barnabas quotes it with words from Psalm 24:4, "someone whose hands are clean and whose heart is pure": a combination no Bible has. It is the key to his argument. No one is now clean in heart, so no one can now keep the day holy (15:6-7). Isaiah 58:13-14 joins right living to the Sabbath too, but as a reason to keep it, not to put it off.

a: in six thousand years the Lord will bring everything to its end
p: Barnabas reads the six days of creation as six thousand years of history, then a seventh-day rest.
b: This is a Christian form of the idea of a "world week": as God made the world in six days and rested on the seventh, so the world will last six thousand years, and then the Son will come and "rest" (15:5). The key is Psalm 90:4 and 2 Peter 3:8: "in the Lord's sight one day is like a thousand years." Barnabas's quoted form ("the Lord's day will be like a thousand years") is close to neither exactly. The site's cards at Revelation 20 set out how churches read the thousand years; Barnabas does not say plainly whether the seventh day is an earthly reign or the eternal rest.

a: then we have been deceived in everything
t: Compared with the Bible: can anyone keep the Sabbath?
p: Barnabas says no one can keep the Sabbath until all things are made new. The Old Testament commands it now.
b: Barnabas argues that keeping the Sabbath holy needs a clean heart, and since no one has one now, the Sabbath can only be kept when "the Lord has made all things new" (15:7). The Old Testament commands the Sabbath for Israel now, every week, as a sign of the covenant (Exodus 31:13-17), and promises blessing to whoever keeps it (Isaiah 56:2). Hebrews 4:9-11 does speak, like Barnabas, of a Sabbath rest still waiting for God's people. So Barnabas goes beyond Hebrews and conflicts with the law's plain command. Christians disagree about whether the Sabbath command binds them; see the site's cards at Exodus 20 and Colossians 2.

a: the beginning of an eighth day
p: After the world's Sabbath comes an "eighth day," the start of a new world. Christians keep it on Sunday.
b: Barnabas gives God words of his own: "It is not the Sabbaths of the present time that I accept, but the one I have made," in which he will make "the beginning of an eighth day, which is the beginning of another world." The eighth day is the day after the Sabbath, the first day of a new week, so it stands both for Sunday and for the new creation. Jesus rose as light was breaking "toward the first day of the week" (Matthew 28:1), and John's Gospel has him appear again "after eight days" (John 20:26).

a: That is why we also keep the eighth day with gladness
p: An early witness that Christians gathered on Sunday, "the eighth day," as a day of joy.
b: "We keep the eighth day" shows a church that already gathered on the day of the resurrection. The New Testament speaks of the first day of the week for the breaking of bread (Acts 20:7), for setting money aside (1 Corinthians 16:2), and "the Lord's day" (Revelation 1:10); the Didache tells believers to gather "on the Lord's day" (Didache 14:1). Barnabas gives the reason: Jesus rose on that day. Whether Christians should rest on Sunday, keep the seventh-day Sabbath, or neither, is a live question among churches; see the site's cards at Revelation 1 and Exodus 20.

a: went up into heaven
t: Rose and went up on the same day?
p: Read one way, Barnabas puts Jesus' ascension on the day he rose. Acts 1:3 has forty days between.
b: The sentence can be read as saying that on the eighth day Jesus rose, appeared, and went up into heaven, all on one day. Luke 24:50-51, read alone, can also seem to place the ascension on Easter evening, while Acts 1:3 says Jesus appeared for forty days first. Barnabas may also mean only that the day of the resurrection began what ended in the ascension, without timing it. The Greek allows both.

a: hoped in the building itself
t: Compared with the Bible: was the Temple a mistake?
p: Barnabas says Israel wrongly trusted the Temple like the pagans. The Bible says God chose it, though he cannot be contained in it.
b: Barnabas says Israel "dedicated him in the temple almost the way the nations do," as if God could be shut up in a shrine. The Bible does warn against trusting the Temple as though it guaranteed safety (Jeremiah 7:4) and says God cannot be contained in a house (1 Kings 8:27; Isaiah 66:1; Acts 7:48-50). But it also says God chose Jerusalem and filled the Temple with his glory (1 Kings 8:10-11; Psalm 132:13-14), and Jesus called it "my Father's house" (John 2:16). So the critique of false trust agrees with the prophets, while the claim that the Temple was a pagan error goes beyond them. See the topic.
r: Jeremiah 7:4; 1 Kings 8:10-11; 1 Kings 8:27; Psalm 132:13-14; Isaiah 66:1; Acts 7:48-50; John 2:16

a: Heaven is a throne for me, and the earth is a stool for my feet
p: The second half is Isaiah 66:1 in the same Greek Stephen quotes in Acts 7:49.
b: "Who measured heaven with a span, or the earth with a handful?" is the Greek of Isaiah 40:12, shortened, with "Was it not I?" added; the site's Isaiah 40:12, from the Hebrew, has "a hand's span." Isaiah 66:1 follows, in the form Stephen quotes in his speech against the Temple (Acts 7:49), whose wording the site's Acts gives. Stephen's speech and Barnabas make the same point: "the Most High does not make his home in what hands have made" (Acts 7:48).

a: those who tore this temple down will build it themselves
t: Rebuilding the Temple and the date of the letter
p: Ladeuze dated the letter to AD 130-131 from 16:3-5, Hadrian's temple at Jerusalem. Lake is unsure.
b: The quotation is close to the Greek of Isaiah 49:17, "you will soon be built by those who tore you down." In 16:4 Barnabas says: "It is happening ... now the very servants of their enemies will build it up again." Lake writes that this "is supposed to refer to the events of 132 A.D.," and that neither this theory nor the one from the ten kings (4:4-5) "is quite satisfactory, but neither date is in itself impossible." Ladeuze (Catholic Encyclopedia) takes the verse as "the command given by Adrian in A.D. 130 for the reconstruction, in honour of Jupiter, of the Temple at Jerusalem," and concludes that the letter "must, consequently, have been written in A.D. 130-131." The Roman historian Cassius Dio writes that the emperor Hadrian founded a city at Jerusalem "naming it Aelia Capitolina, and on the site of the temple of the god he raised a new temple to Jupiter," and that this "brought on a war of no slight importance" (Roman History 69.12), the revolt of Bar Kokhba. The verse can also be read as a hope among Jews that Rome would let them rebuild their own Temple, or as the spiritual building of 16:6-10. The verse cannot settle the date by itself.

a: the very servants of their enemies
p: Greek hypēretai, helpers or underlings. Who they are depends on how 16:4 is dated.
b: "The servants of their enemies" may be Roman officials or soldiers building a pagan temple (if the verse refers to Hadrian), Jews working under Roman permission (if it refers to a hoped-for Jewish rebuilding), or Christians, once servants of the enemy, now built into God's temple (16:7-8). The Greek allows each.
orig: οἱ τῶν ἐχθρῶν ὑπηρέται (hoi tōn echthrōn hypēretai)

a: the Lord will hand over the sheep of the pasture, and their fold and their tower, to destruction
p: Barnabas calls it "Scripture." The words are close to 1 Enoch 89:56 and 89:66, the vision of the sheep.
b: No book of the Bible has these words. They are close to the Animal Vision of 1 Enoch, where Israel is a flock, the Temple a "tower" and Jerusalem a "house": the Lord "left that house of theirs and their tower" and threw the sheep to wild beasts (1 Enoch 89:56), and the beasts "burned that tower and tore down that house" (89:66). Lake's margin points to 1 Enoch 89:55, 66 and 67. Barnabas brings the words in with "the Scripture says." The site's notes on 1 Enoch 89 make the same link. 1 Enoch is Scripture today for the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches.

a: And it happened just as the Lord had said
p: Ladeuze reads this as the Roman destruction of AD 70. The words quoted come from 1 Enoch's vision of an earlier fall.
b: Barnabas says the city, the Temple and the people were handed over "just as the Lord had said." Ladeuze (Catholic Encyclopedia) takes this as the Temple "destroyed by Titus," the Roman destruction of AD 70, and the Jewish Encyclopedia speaks of the Temple as "then recently destroyed by the heathen." Jesus foretold that fall (Mark 13:1-2; Luke 19:41-44; Luke 21:20-24). But the verse does not name Rome, and the "Scripture" it quotes, from 1 Enoch's vision of the sheep, tells of the Babylonian destruction (see the note before this one). Read as AD 70, the verse puts the letter after that year; the words alone do not prove it.

a: when the week is completed
t: A temple built when the week is completed
p: A quotation in no Bible. Lake's margin compares Daniel 9:24-27, the seventy weeks.
b: Barnabas says "it is written" that "when the week is completed, a temple of God will be built in glory in the name of the Lord." No book has this exactly. Lake's margin compares Daniel 9:24-27, the seventy weeks of years. 1 Enoch 91:13 speaks of "a house ... built for the Great King, in glory forever" at the end of a week, and 2 Samuel 7:13 of a house "for my name." Barnabas reads the temple built "in the name" as the believers (16:8).

a: a house of demons
p: Before faith, the heart was a temple "built by hand," full of idols and demons.
b: Barnabas turns the temple picture inward. Before believing, "we" were like a temple "built by hand" (compare Acts 7:48 and the sanctuary "that human hands made" in Mark 14:58), full of idols, "a house of demons." Taken plainly, the "we" means the writer and his readers had once been Gentiles who worshiped idols (compare 1 Thessalonians 1:9; 1 Corinthians 12:2); it may also be the "we" of the whole church. Ladeuze (Catholic Encyclopedia) finds it "impossible to believe that either he or the larger part of his readers were of Jewish origin." The Jewish Encyclopedia, following Güdemann's study of the letter (1876), takes the writer to be "a converted Jew." Jesus' story of the unclean spirit returning to an empty house (Matthew 12:43-45) uses a similar picture.
r: Acts 7:48; Mark 14:58; 1 Thessalonians 1:9; 1 Corinthians 12:2; Matthew 12:43-45; Ephesians 2:1-3

a: the door of the temple, which is the mouth
t: The mouth as the temple door
p: The mouth is the door because God speaks through the believer and the believer confesses.
b: Barnabas lists what lives in the believer: God's word, his call, his wisdom, his commandments, and God himself prophesying. The door of this temple is "the mouth": the confession of faith and the word spoken (Romans 10:9-10; 11:8).

a: As far as it was possible to explain things to you simply
t: The end of the first part, and of the Latin
p: Chapter 17 closes the letter's first part. The one Latin manuscript ends here.
b: Chapters 1-17 are the writer's "knowledge" of Scripture; 18-20 turn to "another knowledge and teaching," the Two Ways. Lake's footnote at 17:2 says that "with the addition of the doxology the Latin version comes here to an end." Lake's introduction says the Latin lacks the Two Ways, and that the question "(perhaps insoluble)" is whether the Latin left it out or the Greek added it: "At present the general opinion is in favour of the former view," that the Latin left it out. On a shorter text of 17:1 itself, see the variant.

a: because they lie hidden in parables
p: Things present and to come lie "in parables": riddles, figures that need explaining.
b: A parabolē here is a figure or riddle, as in 6:10 ("the prophet speaks a parable of the Lord"). Jesus speaks of the secret of the kingdom given to the disciples while to outsiders "everything comes in parables" (Mark 4:11). Barnabas says he has explained the past, but will not write about present and future things, because readers would not understand them. It may be modesty, or a hint at teaching kept for those further along.

a: There are two ways of teaching and of power
t: The Two Ways in Barnabas and the Didache
p: Barnabas 18-20 and Didache 1-5 share a "Two Ways" teaching. Lake gives three views of how they are related.
b: "There are two ways" opens both this section and Didache 1:1. The two run parallel for long stretches, often word for word, though the order differs and each has lines the other lacks. Lake's introduction to the Didache says its first part "is closely connected with the last chapters of the Epistle of Barnabas," and that it is not clear whether Barnabas used the Didache, the Didache used Barnabas, or both used a common source: "probably the majority of scholars incline to the last view, and many think that the common source ... was a Jewish pre-Christian document, used for catechetical purposes," that is, for teaching newcomers. Lake also lists a Latin Doctrina apostolorum among the Didache's witnesses. The picture of two ways is old: Deuteronomy 30:15-19, Psalm 1, Jeremiah 21:8 and Matthew 7:13-14. Where the Greek is the same, the Plain English Translation uses the same English as the site's Didache.

a: one of light and one of darkness
t: Light and darkness, with angels over each
p: Barnabas names the ways "light" and "darkness" and sets angels over them. The Didache says "life" and "death."
b: The Didache calls the ways "life" and "death" (Didache 1:1). Barnabas calls them "light" and "darkness," and sets "light-bringing angels of God" over one and "angels of Satan" over the other. The New Testament uses the same contrast: children of light (Ephesians 5:8; 1 Thessalonians 5:5), walking in the light (1 John 1:5-7), and Satan disguised as "an angel of light" (2 Corinthians 11:14). The site's notes on 1 John compare the Dead Sea Scrolls' Community Rule, which also sets a Prince of Light against an Angel of Darkness.
r: Didache 1:1; Ephesians 5:8; 1 Thessalonians 5:5; 1 John 1:5-7; 2 Corinthians 11:14; John 12:35-36

a: the ruler of the present time of lawlessness
p: The devil rules "the present time"; the Lord rules forever. John calls him "the ruler of this world."
b: Jesus calls the devil "this world's ruler" (John 12:31; compare John 14:30; John 16:11), and Paul "the god of this age" (2 Corinthians 4:4) and "the ruler of the domain of the air" (Ephesians 2:2). Barnabas sets him against the Lord who rules "from eternity and to eternity": the devil's rule is limited to "the present time," the "lawless time" of 4:9 and 15:5.

a: let him hurry there by his works
p: Barnabas urges good works on the way to "the appointed place." Christians read such words in different ways.
b: "The appointed place" is the goal of the road, life with God (compare Acts 1:25, where Judas goes "to his own place"). The road is traveled "by works." The Two Ways is a list of commandments, as the Didache's is, and both end in judgment (19:10; 21:1). Such teaching can be read as the fruit that faith must bear (Ephesians 2:10; James 2:17), or as works counted toward salvation. See the site's cards on faith and works at Romans 3 and James 2.

a: You are to love the one who made you
p: The Didache has "love the God who made you, and your neighbor." Barnabas has love, fear and glory toward God.
b: The Didache opens the way of life with the two great commandments (Didache 1:2; Matthew 22:37-39). Barnabas opens with three: love the one who made you, fear the one who formed you, give glory to the one who ransomed you from death. The neighbor comes later (19:5). "Simple in heart and rich in spirit" is his own; the Didache does not have it.

a: The word of God must never go out from you among people who are impure
p: The meaning is unclear: do not speak God's word among the impure, or do not let it leave you when among them.
b: The Greek is literally "may the word of God not go out of you in the impurity of some." It may mean: do not let God's word leave you (that is, do not forget it) when you are among impure people; or do not speak God's word to those who will defile it (compare Matthew 7:6); or do not let your own speech about God be mixed with impurity. Lake renders it "Thou shalt not let the word of God depart from thee among the impurity of any men." The line has no match in the Didache.

a: You must not murder a child by abortion
p: The Two Ways forbids both abortion and killing newborns, as the Didache does in the same words.
b: The line is word for word in Didache 2:2, and the site uses the same English for both. The Greek phthora means "destruction" or "ruin," here the destruction of an unborn child. Barnabas lists "murderers of children, destroyers of what God has formed" in the way of darkness (20:2). The Bible has no explicit law about abortion; Christians who oppose it point to verses like Psalm 139:13 and Jeremiah 1:5, and the Two Ways forbids it in plain words. Barnabas adds "either" (Greek palin, "again") to the second clause.

a: more than yourself
p: Greek "above your soul." Leviticus 19:18 says "as yourself"; the Two Ways asks for more.
b: Leviticus 19:18 and Jesus say "love your neighbor as yourself" (Matthew 22:39). The Two Ways says "above your soul," more than your own life. The Didache uses the same Greek for those "you are to love more than yourself" (Didache 2:7), and the site follows its English. Barnabas uses the same phrase of his own love for his readers (1:4; 4:6). Compare John 15:13: no one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends.
orig: ὑπὲρ τὴν ψυχήν σου (hyper tēn psychēn sou)

a: You must not be two-minded or a big talker
p: Sinaiticus has "talkative." C and G have "two-tongued," the Didache's word, and G adds the Didache's next line.
b: Lake prints Codex Sinaiticus's glōssōdēs, "talkative" or loose-tongued. Other copies have the Didache's "two-tongued" (Didache 2:4), and G adds a line from the Didache (see the variant). "Two-minded" (dignōmōn) is shared with the Didache.

a: You are to submit to masters as to a figure of God
p: The Two Ways tells slaves to submit and masters to be gentle, as the New Testament household rules do.
b: The lines match Didache 4:10-11 and the household rules of Ephesians 6:5-9 and Colossians 3:22-4:1: slaves are to obey "with fear," and masters are not to threaten, since both have the same Master in heaven. "A figure of God" (typos) is strong: the master stands for God to the slave. Galatians 3:28 and Philemon 16 stand beside such rules in the New Testament; see the topic.
r: Didache 4:10-11; Ephesians 6:5-9; Colossians 3:22-4:1; 1 Peter 2:18; Galatians 3:28; Philemon 16

a: You are to share everything with your neighbor
p: The Two Ways asks believers to share everything, as the first church in Jerusalem did (Acts 4:32).
b: Acts 4:32 says of the first believers, "Not one of them called anything he owned his own." The Two Ways makes it a rule, with a reason: if you share what never decays, share what decays. The Didache says the same, with "your brother" for "your neighbor" and "what never dies" for "what never decays" (Didache 4:8). Paul makes the same argument from spiritual to material sharing (Romans 15:27).

a: like the pupil of your eye
p: The image of Deuteronomy 32:10, Psalm 17:8 and Proverbs 7:2, here for those who teach God's word.
b: God guards Israel "like the pupil of his eye" (Deuteronomy 32:10), and the psalmist asks to be guarded "like the pupil of the eye" (Psalm 17:8). The Two Ways asks believers to love their teachers that way. The Didache instead says to honor the one who speaks God's word "as the Lord" (Didache 4:1).
r: Deuteronomy 32:10; Psalm 17:8; Proverbs 7:2; Didache 4:1; 1 Thessalonians 5:12-13; Hebrews 13:7

a: as a ransom for your sins
t: Working as a ransom for sins
p: The Two Ways says giving from your work is a ransom for your sins. Churches read such words differently.
b: The Didache says the same: "If you have earned something with your hands, you are to give it as ransom for your sins" (Didache 4:6). The idea comes from Jewish wisdom: "Guilt is atoned for by loyal love and faithfulness" (Proverbs 16:6), and in Tobit, "Alms rescue from death, and they cleanse away every sin" (Tobit 12:9). The New Testament says believers were ransomed "with blood of great worth" (1 Peter 1:19). Churches read the Two Ways' words differently; see the site's cards at Proverbs 16.
r: Didache 4:6; Proverbs 16:6; Tobit 12:9; Daniel 4:27; 1 Peter 1:18-19; 1 Peter 4:8

a: You are to confess your sins
p: The Didache says "in the church." Barnabas only says to confess. Churches differ on how.
b: Didache 4:14 says "In the church you are to confess your wrongs"; Barnabas has only "You are to confess your sins." James 5:16 says "confess your sins to each other," and 1 John 1:9 promises forgiveness to those who confess. Whether confession is made to God alone, to the gathered church, or to a priest is a question churches answer differently; the Two Ways does not say.

a: crooked and full of cursing
p: The Didache calls the way of death "evil and full of cursing." Barnabas says "crooked."
b: Didache 5:1 says the way of death "is evil and full of cursing." Barnabas has "crooked" (skolia), the word of Proverbs 2:15 and of the "twisted generation" of Peter's sermon (Acts 2:40). He adds that it is "the way of eternal death with punishment." His list of sins differs from the Didache's in order and in a few items: he has "the haughtiness of power," "transgression" and "no fear of God"; the Didache has theft, false testimony, foul talk and jealousy. Both lists are close to Paul's lists of sins (Galatians 5:19-21; Romans 1:29-31).
r: Didache 5:1; Proverbs 2:15; Acts 2:40; Galatians 5:19-21; Romans 1:29-31; Matthew 7:13

a: They pay no attention to the widow and the orphan
p: A line the Didache lacks. The care of widows and orphans runs through the Bible.
b: Barnabas adds to the Didache's list those who ignore the widow and the orphan. The law and the prophets defend them (Exodus 22:22; Deuteronomy 10:18; Isaiah 1:17, 1:23), and James calls visiting them "clean and unspoiled religion" (James 1:27). He also adds "quick to slander" and "far, far away" for gentleness and endurance. The list ends, as the Didache's does, with "sinners through and through"; the Didache then adds "Children, may you be rescued from all these!" (Didache 5:2), which Barnabas does not have.
r: Didache 5:2; Exodus 22:22-24; Deuteronomy 10:18; Isaiah 1:17; Isaiah 1:23; James 1:27

a: That is why there is a resurrection. That is why there is repayment.
p: The way one walks matters because there will be a resurrection and a judgment.
b: Barnabas closes the Two Ways with its reason: there will be a resurrection and a repayment. Daniel 12:2 speaks of the dead waking, "Some will wake to life without end, and some to shame," and Jesus of "a resurrection that brings life" and "a resurrection that brings judgment" (John 5:29). Paul says each will receive back what he has done (2 Corinthians 5:10). The same thought opened the letter (4:12).

a: those of you who stand above others
t: A word to those in high places
p: The writer asks the well-off or the leaders among his readers to do good to those in need.
b: "Those who stand above others" (Greek hoi hyperechontes) may be the rich or the leaders of the community; Romans 13:1 uses the word for governing authorities, and 1 Timothy 2:2 for "all who hold high office." Barnabas's request is practical: "you have people among you to whom you can do good. Do not fail them." It is one of the few hints in the letter about the community's make-up.

a: Be people taught by God
p: Greek theodidaktoi, the word Paul uses in 1 Thessalonians 4:9.
b: The rare word theodidaktoi, "God-taught," appears in the New Testament only at 1 Thessalonians 4:9, which the site renders "God himself has been your teacher." It echoes Isaiah 54:13 and the words Jesus quotes, "And all of them will be taught by God" (John 6:45). Barnabas, who said he did not write "as a teacher" (1:8), points his readers to the true teacher.

a: While the good vessel is still with you
p: The "vessel" is the body, as long as one is alive. Compare 2 Corinthians 4:7.
b: Barnabas calls the body "the vessel of the spirit" (7:3; 11:9). "While the good vessel is still with you" means while you are still alive in the body, so there is still time. Paul speaks of "this treasure in clay pots" (2 Corinthians 4:7), and 1 Thessalonians 4:4 uses the same Greek word. On "among yourselves" or "in any of them," see the variant.
